title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Genome-wide association studies, or GWAS, have identified many genetic variants associated with complex traits and diseases. However, after identifying a GWAS locus, one important question remains:

Which gene or biological mechanism is responsible for the association?

Many GWAS variants are located in non-coding regions of the genome. They may not directly change protein sequence, but they may influence disease by changing gene regulation. This is where eQTL data becomes useful.
An eQTL is a genetic variant associated with gene expression. If a GWAS variant for a disease is also an eQTL for a nearby gene, it may suggest that the disease association works through altered gene expression.
However, this interpretation is not always safe.
The GWAS signal and the eQTL signal may appear to overlap simply because nearby SNPs are correlated through linkage disequilibrium, or LD. Therefore, visual overlap between GWAS and eQTL signals does not automatically mean that the same causal variant is responsible for both traits.
Colocalization analysis tries to answer this specific question:

Are the GWAS and eQTL signals driven by the same causal variant?

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Genome-wide association studies, or GWAS, have identified many genetic variants associated with complex traits and diseases. However, after identifying a GWAS locus, one important question remains:

Which gene or biological mechanism is responsible for the association?

Many GWAS variants are located in non-coding regions of the genome. They may not directly change protein sequence, but they may influence disease by changing gene regulation. This is where eQTL data becomes useful.
An eQTL is a genetic variant associated with gene expression. If a GWAS variant for a disease is also an eQTL for a nearby gene, it may suggest that the disease association works through altered gene expression.
However, this interpretation is not always safe.
The GWAS signal and the eQTL signal may appear to overlap simply because nearby SNPs are correlated through linkage disequilibrium, or LD. Therefore, visual overlap between GWAS and eQTL signals does not automatically mean that the same causal variant is responsible for both traits.
Colocalization analysis tries to answer this specific question:

Are the GWAS and eQTL signals driven by the same causal variant?

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Why Colocalization is Important
Suppose a GWAS identifies a region associated with depression. In the same region, an eQTL study shows that a nearby SNP is associated with expression of Gene X.
A simple interpretation might be:
Gene X is involved in depression.
But this may be wrong.
There are at least two possible explanations.
First, the same causal variant may influence both Gene X expression and depression risk. This would support a shared biological mechanism.
Second, two different causal variants may exist in the same region. One variant may affect depression risk, while another nearby variant may affect Gene X expression. Because the variants are in LD, the signals may look similar even though they are biologically separate.
Colocalization is designed to distinguish between these two possibilities.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
section: Relationship Between GWAS, eQTL, and Colocalization
text:
Relationship Between GWAS, eQTL, and Colocalization
GWAS asks:
Which variants are associated with disease or trait risk?
eQTL analysis asks:
Which variants are associated with gene expression?
Colocalization asks:
Are the GWAS and eQTL associations likely to share the same causal variant?
A simple post-GWAS workflow is:
GWAS signal
    ↓
Check eQTL signal
    ↓
Run colocalization
    ↓
Prioritize candidate gene
This is why colocalization is now widely used in post-GWAS interpretation, TWAS analysis, Mendelian Randomization, and drug target prioritization.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
The Five Colocalization Hypotheses
The classical Bayesian colocalization framework evaluates five hypotheses.

H0: No Association With Either Trait
There is no evidence that variants in the region are associated with either trait.
Trait 1: no association
Trait 2: no association


H1: Association With Trait 1 Only
Only the first trait is associated in the region.
In many applications, trait 1 is the GWAS trait.
GWAS trait: associated
eQTL trait: not associated


H2: Association With Trait 2 Only
Only the second trait is associated in the region.
In many applications, trait 2 is gene expression.
GWAS trait: not associated
eQTL trait: associated


H3: Both Traits Associated, But Different Causal Variants
Both traits show association in the region, but the evidence suggests that they are driven by different causal variants.
Variant A ──► Disease

Variant B ──► Gene Expression
This means there is no strong evidence for a shared biological mechanism.


H4: Both Traits Associated and Share One Causal Variant
Both traits are associated, and the evidence suggests that the same causal variant drives both signals.
Variant ──► Gene Expression
       └──► Disease Risk
This is the main colocalization scenario researchers usually hope to find.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
The Most Important Quantity: PP.H4
The coloc package reports posterior probabilities for each hypothesis.
The most important quantity is usually:
PP.H4.abf
This means the posterior probability that both traits share the same causal variant.
A rough interpretation is:
PP.H4 < 0.50       weak evidence for colocalization
PP.H4 0.50–0.80    moderate evidence
PP.H4 > 0.80       strong evidence
PP.H4 > 0.90       very strong evidence
These are not universal rules. The threshold depends on the study design, sample size, prior assumptions, and biological context.



## Install and Load Required Packages


# Install packages if needed
# install.packages("coloc")
# install.packages("ggplot2")
# install.packages("dplyr")

library(coloc)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

text:
Simulated Example Using the coloc Package
In this example, we simulate 100 SNPs from one genomic region. We create one GWAS signal and one eQTL signal. Both are given a strong effect at SNP 50, representing a simplified shared causal variant.
This is a toy example, but it helps us understand what the coloc.abf() function needs as input.

set.seed(42)

# Number of SNPs in the region
n_snps <- 100

# SNP IDs and positions
snp_ids <- paste0("rs", 1:n_snps)
position <- 1:n_snps

# Minor allele frequencies
maf <- runif(n_snps, min = 0.05, max = 0.50)

# Standard errors
gwas_se <- rep(0.05, n_snps)
eqtl_se <- rep(0.05, n_snps)

# Simulate small background effects
gwas_beta <- rnorm(n_snps, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)
eqtl_beta <- rnorm(n_snps, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)

# Add one shared causal signal at SNP 50
gwas_beta[50] <- 0.50
eqtl_beta[50] <- 0.60

# Create a data frame for visualization
sim_data <- data.frame(
  SNP = snp_ids,
  Position = position,
  MAF = maf,
  GWAS_Beta = gwas_beta,
  eQTL_Beta = eqtl_beta,
  GWAS_SE = gwas_se,
  eQTL_SE = eqtl_se
)

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Prepare Data for coloc
The coloc.abf() function needs the GWAS and eQTL data as lists.
For the GWAS dataset, we use:
type = "cc"
because the GWAS trait is treated as a case-control disease outcome.
For the eQTL dataset, we use:
type = "quant"
because gene expression is a quantitative trait.
For quantitative traits, coloc needs either sdY, or enough information to estimate it. Here we set:
sdY = 1
because this is a simulated example.

gwas_data <- list(
  beta = gwas_beta,
  varbeta = gwas_se^2,
  snp = snp_ids,
  MAF = maf,
  type = "cc",
  s = 0.30,
  N = 50000
)

eqtl_data <- list(
  beta = eqtl_beta,
  varbeta = eqtl_se^2,
  snp = snp_ids,
  MAF = maf,
  type = "quant",
  N = 1000,
  sdY = 1
)



## Run Colocalization Analysis

coloc_result <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = gwas_data,
  dataset2 = eqtl_data
)

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Understanding H3 vs H4
The distinction between H3 and H4 is one of the most important concepts in colocalization analysis.
A common misconception is that overlapping GWAS and eQTL association peaks automatically imply that the same variant is responsible for both signals. Because nearby variants are often correlated through LD, this assumption can be incorrect.

H3: Different Causal Variants
A high posterior probability for H3 means that both traits are associated in the region, but they are probably driven by different causal variants.
Conceptually:
Variant A ──► Disease

Variant B ──► Gene Expression
In this case, the region contains both a GWAS signal and an eQTL signal, but there is little evidence that the gene expression change explains the disease association.


H4: Shared Causal Variant
A high posterior probability for H4 means that the same variant is likely responsible for both the GWAS and eQTL associations.
Conceptually:
Variant
    │
    ├──► Gene Expression
    │
    └──► Disease Risk
This is often interpreted as evidence that altered gene expression may be involved in disease biology.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Simulating a Different-Causal-Variant Scenario
Now we simulate a second example where the GWAS signal is strongest at SNP 40 and the eQTL signal is strongest at SNP 70.
This represents a situation where both traits are associated in the region, but likely through different causal variants.

set.seed(123)

gwas_beta_diff <- rnorm(n_snps, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)
eqtl_beta_diff <- rnorm(n_snps, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)

# Different causal SNPs
gwas_beta_diff[40] <- 0.50
eqtl_beta_diff[70] <- 0.60

diff_data <- data.frame(
  SNP = snp_ids,
  Position = position,
  GWAS_Beta = gwas_beta_diff,
  eQTL_Beta = eqtl_beta_diff
)

ggplot(diff_data, aes(x = Position)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = abs(GWAS_Beta), color = "GWAS"), size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = abs(eQTL_Beta), color = "eQTL"), size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 40, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 70, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(
    title = "Different Causal Variant Scenario",
    subtitle = "GWAS peak and eQTL peak occur at different SNPs",
    x = "SNP Position",
    y = "Absolute Effect Size",
    color = "Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









gwas_data_diff <- list(
  beta = gwas_beta_diff,
  varbeta = gwas_se^2,
  snp = snp_ids,
  MAF = maf,
  type = "cc",
  s = 0.30,
  N = 50000
)

eqtl_data_diff <- list(
  beta = eqtl_beta_diff,
  varbeta = eqtl_se^2,
  snp = snp_ids,
  MAF = maf,
  type = "quant",
  N = 1000,
  sdY = 1
)

coloc_result_diff <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = gwas_data_diff,
  dataset2 = eqtl_data_diff
)

coloc_result_diff$summary

PP.H0.abf PP.H1.abf PP.H2.abf PP.H3.abf PP.H4.abf

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
section: Why Visual Overlap Is Not Enough
text:
Why Visual Overlap Is Not Enough
It is tempting to look at two regional plots and decide whether the peaks overlap. However, nearby SNPs are often correlated because of LD.
This means two different causal variants can produce similar association patterns.
Therefore, colocalization is stronger than visual inspection because it formally compares hypotheses about shared and distinct causal variants.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Colocalization and TWAS
Transcriptome-wide association studies, or TWAS, test whether genetically predicted gene expression is associated with a trait.
A simplified TWAS idea is:
Genetic variants ──► Predicted gene expression ──► Disease trait
However, TWAS signals can arise because of LD or multiple nearby genes with correlated expression. Therefore, a significant TWAS result does not automatically prove that the gene is causal.
Colocalization is often used alongside TWAS.
A stronger interpretation is possible when:
Gene is significant in TWAS
+
GWAS and eQTL signals colocalize
This combination gives more confidence that the gene may be biologically relevant.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Colocalization and Mendelian Randomization
Mendelian Randomization, or MR, can be used to test whether genetically predicted exposure affects an outcome.
For gene expression studies, the exposure may be expression of a gene and the outcome may be disease risk.
MR asks:
Does gene expression causally affect disease?
Colocalization asks:
Do gene expression and disease share the same causal variant?
These are related but different questions.
If MR suggests a causal effect but colocalization is weak, the MR result may be driven by LD or pleiotropy. Therefore, colocalization is often an important sensitivity analysis for expression-based MR.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Limitations of Classical Colocalization
The classical coloc method assumes one causal variant per region for each trait. This assumption may not always hold.
Real genetic loci can contain multiple independent signals.
Other limitations include:
Incorrect LD structure
Poor variant coverage
Allele harmonization errors
Different ancestry between datasets
Weak eQTL sample size
Tissue mismatch
Multiple causal variants
Because of these limitations, colocalization should not be interpreted mechanically. A high PP.H4 is useful evidence, but it should be considered together with biology, tissue relevance, fine-mapping, and replication.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Modern Extensions
Several newer methods extend classical colocalization.

SuSiE-Coloc
SuSiE-coloc combines colocalization with fine-mapping and can handle multiple causal signals in a region.


eCAVIAR
eCAVIAR jointly models colocalization and fine-mapping while accounting for LD.


fastENLOC
fastENLOC is designed for large-scale enrichment and colocalization analyses across many loci and molecular traits.
These methods are useful when the simple one-causal-variant assumption is unrealistic.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Practical Interpretation Checklist
When interpreting colocalization results, I would check the following:
1. Is there a strong GWAS signal in the region?
2. Is there a strong eQTL signal in the same tissue?
3. Are the alleles harmonized correctly?
4. Are the GWAS and eQTL datasets ancestry-matched?
5. Is PP.H4 high?
6. Is PP.H3 also high?
7. Is the tissue biologically relevant?
8. Does the result agree with TWAS, MR, or functional evidence?
A high PP.H4 is helpful, but it is not the final proof of causality.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
Summary
Colocalization analysis is a key method in post-GWAS interpretation. It helps determine whether two association signals, such as a disease GWAS signal and an eQTL signal, are likely to share the same causal variant.
The main idea is simple but important:
Overlapping association signals do not automatically mean shared causality.
The coloc framework evaluates five hypotheses: H0, H1, H2, H3, and H4. Among these, H4 is usually the most important because it represents evidence that both traits share one causal variant.
In practical genetic studies, colocalization is often used together with eQTL analysis, TWAS, MR, and fine-mapping to prioritize genes and biological mechanisms.
For researchers working with GWAS, FinnGen, UK Biobank, GTEx, PsychENCODE, or other molecular QTL resources, colocalization is one of the most useful tools for moving from statistical association toward biological interpretation.

title: Colocalization Analysis in Statistical Genetics: Theory and Practical Example in R
text:
References
Giambartolomei, C. et al. Bayesian test for colocalisation between pairs of genetic association studies using summary statistics. PLoS Genetics, 2014.
Wallace, C. A more accurate method for colocalisation analysis allowing for multiple causal variants. PLoS Genetics, 2021.
GTEx Consortium. The GTEx Consortium atlas of genetic regulatory effects across human tissues. Science, 2020.
Hormozdiari, F. et al. Colocalization of GWAS and eQTL signals detects target genes. American Journal of Human Genetics, 2016.

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
When people think about evolution, they often think about natural selection.
Natural selection explains how advantageous genetic variants become more common because they improve survival or reproduction.
However, natural selection is not the only force driving evolution.
Even in the complete absence of selection, allele frequencies can change over time simply because populations are finite.
This phenomenon is called genetic drift.
Genetic drift is one of the most fundamental concepts in population genetics because it explains:
Understanding drift is essential for modern genomics, GWAS, evolutionary biology, conservation genetics, and statistical genetics.
In this tutorial we will study:

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
0.1 Interpretation
Notice the dramatic difference.
For:
\[
N=20
\]
the allele frequency may rapidly reach fixation or extinction.
For:
\[
N=1000
\]
the frequency remains close to its initial value.
This directly verifies the variance theorem.

0.1.1 Quantifying Drift Variability
Instead of looking at one trajectory, we can measure variance across many replicate populations.

population_sizes = [
    20,
    50,
    100,
    500,
    1000
]

variances=[]

for N in population_sizes:

    final_freqs=[]

    for _ in range(1000):

        traj = simulate_drift(
            N=N,
            p0=0.5,
            generations=100
        )

        final_freqs.append(
            traj[-1]
        )

    variances.append(
        np.var(final_freqs)
    )


plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

plt.plot(
    population_sizes,
    variances,
    marker="o",
    linewidth=3
)

plt.xlabel("Population Size")
plt.ylabel("Variance of Final Allele Frequency")

plt.title(
    "Drift Variance Decreases With Population Size"
)

plt.show()

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
0.2 Experiment 2: Initial Allele Frequency
The fixation theorem states:
\[
P(Fixation)=p_0
\]
where, \(p_0\) is the initial allele frequency.
We first visualize trajectories starting from different frequencies.

starting_frequencies = [
    0.1,
    0.3,
    0.5,
    0.7,
    0.9
]

plt.figure(figsize=(12,7))

for p0 in starting_frequencies:

    traj = simulate_drift(
        N=100,
        p0=p0,
        generations=200
    )

    plt.plot(
        traj,
        label=f"p0={p0}"
    )

plt.xlabel("Generation")
plt.ylabel("Allele Frequency")

plt.title(
    "Effect of Initial Allele Frequency"
)

plt.legend()

plt.show()









0.2.1 Interpretation
Alleles beginning near \(p=1\) have a much greater chance of fixation.
Alleles beginning near \(p=0\)
have a much greater chance of loss.


0.2.2 Experiment 3: Verifying the Fixation Theorem
One of the most elegant results in population genetics states \(P(Fixation)=p_0\) .
We now verify this experimentally.

def estimate_fixation_probability(
    p0,
    N=100,
    generations=1000,
    n_replicates=1000
):

    fixation_count=0

    for _ in range(n_replicates):

        traj = simulate_drift(
            N=N,
            p0=p0,
            generations=generations
        )

        if traj[-1] == 1:
            fixation_count += 1

    return fixation_count/n_replicates

p0_values = np.arange(
    0.05,
    1.0,
    0.05
)

estimated_probs=[]

for p0 in p0_values:

    estimated_probs.append(
        estimate_fixation_probability(
            p0=p0,
            N=100,
            generations=1000,
            n_replicates=500
        )
    )



plt.figure(figsize=(8,8))

plt.plot(
    p0_values,
    p0_values,
    linewidth=3,
    label="Theory"
)

plt.scatter(
    p0_values,
    estimated_probs,
    s=70,
    label="Simulation"
)

plt.xlabel("Initial Frequency")
plt.ylabel("Fixation Probability")

plt.title(
    "Experimental Verification of the Fixation Theorem"
)

plt.legend()

plt.show()










0.2.3 Interpretation
The simulation closely follows the theoretical prediction:
\[
P(Fixation)=p_0
\]
This is one of the most important theorems in neutral evolution.


0.2.4 Experiment 4: Multiple SNP Simulation
Real genomes contain millions of SNPs.
Instead of tracking a single locus, we simulate many SNPs simultaneously.

# Creating 1,000 Independent SNPs


n_snps = 1000

initial_freqs = np.random.uniform(
    0.05,
    0.95,
    n_snps
)

final_freqs=[]

for p0 in initial_freqs:

    traj = simulate_drift(
        N=100,
        p0=p0,
        generations=200
    )

    final_freqs.append(
        traj[-1]
    )


# Visualizing Frequency Changes

plt.figure(figsize=(12,6))

plt.hist(
    initial_freqs,
    bins=30,
    alpha=0.6,
    label="Initial Frequencies"
)

plt.hist(
    final_freqs,
    bins=30,
    alpha=0.6,
    label="Final Frequencies"
)

plt.xlabel("Allele Frequency")
plt.ylabel("Number of SNPs")

plt.title(
    "Genetic Drift Reshapes the Frequency Spectrum"
)

plt.legend()

plt.show()











0.2.5 Interpretation
Initially, frequencies were nearly uniform.
After drift:

More SNPs accumulate near 0
More SNPs accumulate near 1
Intermediate frequencies become less common

This is a hallmark of neutral evolution.


0.2.6 Experiment 5: SNP Loss and Fixation
How many SNPs become fixed or lost?



lost=0
fixed=0

for p in final_freqs:

    if p == 0:
        lost += 1

    elif p == 1:
        fixed += 1

print("Lost SNPs:", lost)
print("Fixed SNPs:", fixed)


# Visualization


categories = [
    "Lost",
    "Fixed",
    "Segregating"
]

counts = [
    lost,
    fixed,
    len(final_freqs)-lost-fixed
]

plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))

plt.bar(
    categories,
    counts
)

plt.ylabel("Number of SNPs")

plt.title(
    "Fate of SNPs After Drift"
)

plt.show()

Lost SNPs: 313
Fixed SNPs: 285











0.2.7 Experiment 6: Number of SNPs Matters
Now repeat the experiment using increasingly larger numbers of SNPs.


snp_counts = [
    100,
    500,
    1000,
    5000
]

fixed_counts=[]
lost_counts=[]

for n_snps in snp_counts:

    fixed=0
    lost=0

    freqs=np.random.uniform(
        0.05,
        0.95,
        n_snps
    )

    for p0 in freqs:

        traj=simulate_drift(
            N=50,
            p0=p0,
            generations=300
        )

        if traj[-1]==1:
            fixed += 1

        elif traj[-1]==0:
            lost += 1

    fixed_counts.append(fixed)
    lost_counts.append(lost)

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

plt.plot(
    snp_counts,
    fixed_counts,
    marker="o",
    linewidth=3,
    label="Fixed"
)

plt.plot(
    snp_counts,
    lost_counts,
    marker="o",
    linewidth=3,
    label="Lost"
)

plt.xlabel("Number of SNPs")
plt.ylabel("Count")

plt.title(
    "Genome-Wide Consequences of Drift"
)

plt.legend()

plt.show()











0.2.8 Interpretation
As the number of SNPs increases:

More variants become fixed
More variants become lost
Overall diversity declines



0.2.9 Experiment 7: Sampling Error Versus Genetic Drift
In GWAS we rarely observe the entire population.
Instead we estimate allele frequencies from samples.
Suppose the true frequency is \(p=0.30\).


0.2.10 Simulating Sampling Error


true_frequency = 0.30

sample_sizes = [
    20,
    50,
    100,
    500,
    1000,
    5000
]

sampling_std=[]

for n in sample_sizes:

    estimates=[]

    for _ in range(5000):

        count = np.random.binomial(
            n,
            true_frequency
        )

        estimates.append(
            count/n
        )

    sampling_std.append(
        np.std(estimates)
    )

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

plt.plot(
    sample_sizes,
    sampling_std,
    marker="o",
    linewidth=3
)

plt.xlabel("Sample Size")
plt.ylabel("Standard Deviation")

plt.title(
    "Sampling Error Decreases With Sample Size"
)

plt.show()












0.2.11 Interpretation
Larger studies produce more precise allele frequency estimates.
This randomness is not genetic drift.
Instead it is statistical sampling error.


0.2.12 Genetic Drift vs Sampling Error



Genetic Drift
Sampling Error




Biological process
Measurement process


Occurs across generations
Occurs during data collection


Changes true frequency
Changes estimated frequency


Evolutionary phenomenon
Statistical phenomenon



Understanding this distinction is essential in GWAS and population genetics.


0.2.13 Experiment 8: Distribution of Frequency Estimates


sample_size = 50

estimates=[]

for _ in range(10000):

    count=np.random.binomial(
        sample_size,
        true_frequency
    )

    estimates.append(
        count/sample_size
    )

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

plt.hist(
    estimates,
    bins=40
)

plt.axvline(
    true_frequency,
    linestyle="--"
)

plt.xlabel("Estimated Frequency")
plt.ylabel("Count")

plt.title(
    "Sampling Distribution of Allele Frequency Estimates"
)

plt.show()











0.2.14 Interpretation
Even though the true frequency remains fixed at:
\[
p=0.30
\]
individual samples produce different estimates.
This is exactly why larger cohorts improve statistical power.


0.2.15 Summary
In this section we experimentally demonstrated:

Small populations drift faster.
Large populations are more stable.
Fixation probability equals starting frequency.
Drift pushes SNPs toward fixation and extinction.
Diversity decreases across the genome.
Sample size affects precision of allele-frequency estimation.
Sampling error and genetic drift are fundamentally different processes.

Genome-wide simulations
Heterozygosity decay

Bottlenecks
Founder effects
Population structure

0.2.16 Genome-Wide Consequences of Genetic Drift
So far we have studied drift at the level of individual SNPs.
Real genomes contain millions of variants.
Over evolutionary time, drift acts simultaneously on all of them.
The cumulative effect produces:

Loss of genetic diversity
Population differentiation
Founder effects
Population bottlenecks
Changes in allele frequency spectra

Many patterns observed in modern genomics can be understood through drift alone.


0.2.17 Heterozygosity
One of the most important measures of genetic diversity is heterozygosity.
For a biallelic SNP:
\[
H = 2p(1-p)
\]
where:

(p) = frequency of allele A
(1-p) = frequency of allele a



0.2.18 Maximum Heterozygosity
The maximum occurs when:
\[
p=0.5
\]
because:
\[
H=2(0.5)(0.5)=0.5
\]
The minimum occurs when:
\[
p=0
\]
or
\[
p=1
\]
because:
\[
H=0
\]
At fixation, all diversity disappears.

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
1.1 Interpretation
The populations began identically.
Drift alone created differences.
This is the foundation of population structure.

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
1.2 Connection to FST
Population differentiation is often measured using:
\[
F_{ST}
\]
which quantifies how much allele frequencies differ between populations.
Drift increases:
\[
F_{ST}
\]
over time.

1.2.1 Why GWAS Researchers Care About Drift
Modern GWAS datasets contain individuals from populations with different demographic histories.
Drift can create allele-frequency differences unrelated to disease.

1.2.1.1 Example
Suppose:
Population A:
\[
p=0.7
\]
Population B:
\[
p=0.3
\]
for a SNP.
If disease prevalence also differs between populations, a naive GWAS may falsely associate the SNP with disease.


1.2.1.2 Confounding
This phenomenon is called:
Population stratification.
Drift is one of its major causes.



1.2.2 How GWAS Controls Drift Effects
Modern studies use:

Principal Components Analysis (PCA)
Linear Mixed Models
Genetic Relationship Matrices
Ancestry Adjustment

to account for population structure.


1.2.3 Connection to FinnGen
Finnish populations experienced:

Founder events
Bottlenecks
Relative isolation

Consequently:

Some rare variants became common
Certain disease alleles increased in frequency

This is known as the Finnish Disease Heritage.


1.2.4 Connection to UK Biobank
UK Biobank contains:

Multiple ancestry groups
Geographic structure
Historical demographic differences

These produce subtle allele-frequency differences caused partly by drift.


1.2.5 Connection to Polygenic Scores
Polygenic scores depend on allele frequencies.
Since drift changes frequencies:

Prediction accuracy changes across populations
Transferability decreases
Ancestry matching becomes important


Genetic drift is random evolution caused by finite populations.
Drift eventually causes fixation or extinction.
Small populations drift faster than large populations.
Heterozygosity decreases through time.
Effective population size determines drift strength.
Bottlenecks accelerate drift.
Founder effects reshape genetic variation.
Drift creates population structure.
Drift contributes to FST.
Drift influences GWAS, polygenic scores, and demographic inference.

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
1.3 Summary
One of the most surprising lessons in population genetics is that evolution does not always require selection.
Randomness alone can dramatically reshape genomes.
Given enough time, drift can:

Eliminate variants
Fix variants
Reduce diversity
Differentiate populations

Many genomic patterns observed today arise not because some variants were better than others, but simply because finite populations are subject to chance.
Understanding genetic drift is therefore essential for evolutionary biology, statistical genetics, genomics, and modern precision medicine.

title: Genetic Drift and Fixation: Understanding Evolution Through Randomness
text:
0.1 The Wright-Fisher Model
The Wright-Fisher model is the classical mathematical model of genetic drift.
Assumptions:

Constant population size
Diploid individuals
Random mating
No mutation
No migration
No selection
Non-overlapping generations

Suppose:
\[
N
\]
is the number of diploid individuals.
There are:
\[
2N
\]
gene copies.

0.1.1 Sampling the Next Generation
Suppose allele A has frequency:
\[
p_t
\]
in generation:
\[
t
\]
The number of copies of allele A in the next generation follows:
\[
X_{t+1}
\sim
Binomial(2N,p_t)
\]
The allele frequency becomes:
\[
p_{t+1}
=
\frac{X_{t+1}}{2N}
\]
This simple equation forms the foundation of modern population genetics.


0.1.2 Important Theorem 1: Drift Has No Direction
For a neutral allele:
\[
E[p_{t+1}\mid p_t]
=
p_t
\]
Interpretation:
On average, allele frequencies do not systematically increase or decrease.
Drift is unbiased.
However, individual populations may behave very differently.


0.1.3 Important Theorem 2: Variance of Drift
The variance is:
\[
Var(p_{t+1}\mid p_t)
=
\frac{p_t(1-p_t)}{2N}
\]
This equation reveals an important biological fact:
Drift becomes stronger as population size decreases.


0.1.4 Why Small Populations Drift Faster
Suppose:
\[
p_t=0.5
\]
For
\[
N=20
\]
the variance becomes:
\[
\frac{0.5\times0.5}{40}
=
0.00625
\]
For
\[
N=1000
\]
the variance becomes:
\[
\frac{0.5\times0.5}{2000}
=
0.000125
\]
The smaller population experiences much larger fluctuations.


0.1.5 Important Theorem 3: Fixation Probability
One of the most beautiful results in population genetics states:
For a neutral allele:
\[
P(Fixation)=p_0
\]
where
\[
p_0
\]
is the starting frequency.
Examples:



Initial Frequency
Fixation Probability




0.1
10%


0.2
20%


0.5
50%


0.8
80%





0.1.6 New Mutations
A new mutation begins as a single copy.
In a diploid population:
\[
p_0
=
\frac{1}{2N}
\]
Therefore:
\[
P(Fixation)
=
\frac{1}{2N}
\]
Example:
For
\[
N=1000
\]
\[
P(Fixation)
=
0.0005
\]
Only 0.05%.
Most neutral mutations disappear.


0.1.7 Important Theorem 4: Heterozygosity Decay
Drift reduces genetic diversity.
Expected heterozygosity after t generations:
\[
H_t
=
H_0
\left(
1-\frac{1}{2N}
\right)^t
\]
This explains why isolated populations lose diversity over time.

# Setting Up Python


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(42)



0.1.8 Simulating the Wright-Fisher Model
We now implement the model directly.

def simulate_drift(
    N=100,
    p0=0.5,
    generations=100
):

    p = p0

    trajectory = [p]

    for _ in range(generations):

        count_A = np.random.binomial(
            2*N,
            p
        )

        p = count_A/(2*N)

        trajectory.append(p)

        if p == 0 or p == 1:

            trajectory.extend(
                [p]*(generations-len(trajectory)+1)
            )

            break

    return np.array(trajectory)


# Simulating One Population


trajectory = simulate_drift(
    N=100,
    p0=0.5,
    generations=200
)




# Visualizing Drift


plt.figure(figsize=(12,6))

plt.plot(
    trajectory,
    linewidth=2
)

plt.axhline(
    0,
    linestyle="--"
)

plt.axhline(
    1,
    linestyle="--"
)

plt.xlabel("Generation")
plt.ylabel("Allele Frequency")

plt.title(
    "Single Wright-Fisher Trajectory"
)

plt.ylim(
    -0.05,
    1.05
)

plt.show()










0.1.9 Interpreting the Plot
Notice:

Frequency fluctuates randomly
No directional trend exists
Changes occur despite no selection
Eventually fixation or extinction may occur

This randomness is the hallmark of genetic drift.


0.1.10 Simulating Multiple Populations
The true power of drift appears when we simulate many populations with identical starting conditions.


def simulate_many_populations(
    N=100,
    p0=0.5,
    generations=200,
    n_replicates=50
):

    trajectories=[]

    for _ in range(n_replicates):

        traj = simulate_drift(
            N,
            p0,
            generations
        )

        trajectories.append(traj)

    return np.array(trajectories)

trajectories = simulate_many_populations(
    N=100,
    p0=0.5,
    generations=200,
    n_replicates=50
)

plt.figure(figsize=(12,7))

for traj in trajectories:

    plt.plot(
        traj,
        alpha=0.3
    )

plt.xlabel("Generation")
plt.ylabel("Allele Frequency")

plt.title(
    "50 Independent Populations Starting at p=0.5"
)

plt.ylim(
    -0.05,
    1.05
)

plt.show()










0.1.11 Interpretation
All populations began with: $ p_0=0.5$.
Yet they diverged dramatically.
Some populations moved upward.
Some moved downward.
Some approached fixation.
Some approached extinction.
This illustrates a central lesson:

Evolutionary outcomes can differ substantially even when populations start under identical conditions.



0.1.12 Summary
In this first part we learned:

What genetic drift is
Why finite populations matter
What fixation means
The Wright-Fisher model
Classical theorems of drift
Why small populations drift faster
How to simulate allele-frequency trajectories

In Part 2 we will move beyond a single SNP and systematically investigate:

Population size effects
Initial allele frequency effects
Fixation probability verification
Multiple SNP simulations
Sample size effects
Allele frequency spectra



0.1.13 Experimental Exploration of Genetic Drift
In Part 1, we simulated a single SNP evolving under neutral genetic drift.
Now we move toward a more realistic population genetics framework by asking:

What happens when population size changes?
What happens when initial allele frequency changes?
Can we experimentally verify the fixation theorem?
What happens when thousands of SNPs evolve simultaneously?
How does sample size affect allele frequency estimates?
How does drift reshape the allele frequency spectrum?

These experiments mirror questions encountered in modern statistical genetics and genomics.


0.1.14 Experiment 1: Effect of Population Size
Recall the variance theorem:
\[
Var(p_{t+1}|p_t)
=
\frac{p_t(1-p_t)}{2N}
\]
The denominator contains population size:
\[
N
\]
Therefore:

Small populations should drift rapidly.
Large populations should drift slowly.



0.1.15 Simulating Different Population Sizes


population_sizes = [
    20,
    50,
    100,
    500,
    1000
]

plt.figure(figsize=(12,7))

for N in population_sizes:

    traj = simulate_drift(
        N=N,
        p0=0.5,
        generations=200
    )

    plt.plot(
        traj,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"N={N}"
    )

plt.xlabel("Generation")
plt.ylabel("Allele Frequency")

plt.title(
    "Effect of Population Size on Genetic Drift"
)

plt.legend()

plt.ylim(
    -0.05,
    1.05
)

plt.show()

text:
1.1 Should the MAF Threshold Change in a Larger Study?
Yes, possibly.
In a much larger sample, such as 100,000 or 500,000 individuals, we may have enough power to analyze rarer variants.
For example:



Sample Size
Reasonable MAF threshold




2,000
1% or 5%


50,000
0.5% or 1%


500,000
0.1% may be possible



However, rare variant analysis often requires additional care, such as burden tests or sequence-level QC.

1.1.1 Step 1.4: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium gives expected genotype frequencies under random mating.
For allele frequency:
\[
p
\]
the expected genotype frequencies are:
\[
p^2
\]
\[
2p(1-p)
\]
\[
(1-p)^2
\]
Strong deviation from HWE can indicate:

genotyping error
population stratification
inbreeding
selection
true disease association in case-control data

Remove SNPs with HWE p-value below:
\[
1 \times 10^{-6}
\]
plink --bfile study1_maf \
  --hwe 1e-6 \
  --make-bed \
  --out study1_qc_snps

section: 1.2 Why Test HWE Only in Controls for Case-Control Studies?
text:
1.2 Why Test HWE Only in Controls for Case-Control Studies?
In case-control studies, a truly disease-associated SNP may deviate from HWE among cases.
If we test HWE in all individuals or in cases, we may accidentally remove true disease signals.
Therefore, for case-control GWAS, HWE filtering is often performed in controls only.

1.2.1 Step 1.5: Individual Missingness
After SNP QC, we check missingness per individual.
Some individuals may have poor DNA quality and many missing genotypes.
Remove individuals missing more than 2% of genotypes:
plink --bfile study1_qc_snps \
  --mind 0.02 \
  --make-bed \
  --out study1_qc_mind
Explanation:



Flag
Meaning




--mind 0.02
Remove individuals with missingness > 2%





1.2.2 Step 1.6: Heterozygosity Check
Heterozygosity is the proportion of SNPs where an individual carries two different alleles.
Individuals with unusually high heterozygosity may indicate:

sample contamination
DNA mixture
technical artifacts

Individuals with unusually low heterozygosity may indicate:

inbreeding
long runs of homozygosity
poor genotype calling

Compute heterozygosity:
plink --bfile study1_qc_mind \
  --het \
  --out study1_het
Inspect:
head study1_het.het
Important columns:



Column
Meaning




O(HOM)
Observed homozygous genotypes


E(HOM)
Expected homozygous genotypes


N(NM)
Number of non-missing genotypes


F
Inbreeding coefficient estimate

12.1 Part 2: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) and Population Stratification

12.1.0.1 Why Do We Need PCA?
Suppose we perform a GWAS for a disease.
Imagine:

Group A has ancestry from Northern Europe
Group B has ancestry from Southern Europe

Now suppose:

Disease prevalence differs between groups
Allele frequencies differ between groups

A SNP can appear associated with disease simply because ancestry differs.
This creates a false positive association.
This phenomenon is called:


12.1.1 Population Stratification
Population stratification is one of the largest sources of false positives in GWAS.
A GWAS can produce apparently significant associations even when no causal effect exists.

12.1.1.1 Example
Suppose:



Population
Disease Rate
Allele Frequency




Population A
10%
0.20


Population B
40%
0.80



Even if the SNP has nothing to do with disease:

cases contain more individuals from Population B
controls contain more individuals from Population A

The SNP becomes associated with disease.
The association is completely spurious.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
Why are people different from one another?
Why are some individuals taller, stronger, more intelligent, or more susceptible to diseases than others?
Why do some siblings resemble each other strongly, while others seem remarkably different?
These questions have fascinated scientists for over a century. Modern statistical genetics attempts to answer these questions by partitioning the observed variation in a trait into genetic and environmental components.
The central concept behind this endeavor is heritability.
In this tutorial, we will start from the basic concepts and gradually build toward Structural Equation Models (SEM), ACE models, and genomic heritability.






Note



Heritability is one of the most frequently misunderstood concepts in genetics. It describes variation within a population, not the extent to which a trait is “genetic” for an individual.






Heritability measures how much of the observed variation in a trait is attributable to genetic differences among individuals.
Importantly:

Heritability is a property of a population, not an individual.

A common misunderstanding is that a heritability of 70% means that 70% of a person’s trait is genetic.
This is incorrect.
Instead, a heritability estimate of 70% means:

70% of the variation observed across individuals in a population can be statistically attributed to genetic differences.





Heritability is fundamentally about explaining variance.
Suppose we measure height in 10,000 individuals.
Some individuals are:

Very short
Average height
Very tall

The spread of these measurements is called the phenotypic variance.
We denote this as:
\[
V_P
\]
where:

\(V\) = variance
\(P\) = phenotype





One of the central ideas in quantitative genetics is that phenotypic variance can be decomposed into genetic and environmental components.
\[
V_P = V_G + V_E
\]
where:



Component
Meaning




\(V_P\)
Phenotypic variance


\(V_G\)
Genetic variance


\(V_E\)
Environmental variance



This simple equation forms the foundation of quantitative genetics.




Imagine we observe the following heights:
160 cm
165 cm
170 cm
175 cm
180 cm
The mean height is:
\[
170 \text{ cm}
\]
The variance measures how much individuals deviate from this average.
Now imagine:

Genetics explains half of this variation
Environment explains the other half

Then:
\[
V_G = 0.5
\]
\[
V_E = 0.5
\]
and therefore:
\[
V_P = 1.0
\]




Heritability is defined as:
\[
h^2 = \frac{V_G}{V_P}
\]
This quantity ranges between:
\[
0 \le h^2 \le 1
\]
or equivalently:
\[
0\% \le h^2 \le 100\%
\]




Suppose:
\[
h^2 = 0.80
\]
Interpretation:

80% of the observed variation in the trait is attributable to genetic differences among individuals.

The remaining:
\[
20\%
\]
is attributable to environmental factors.




High heritability does not imply immutability.
For example, human height has a heritability of approximately:
\[
h^2 \approx 0.80
\]
Yet average height increased substantially during the 20th century due to improvements in:

Nutrition
Healthcare
Sanitation
Living conditions

Environmental changes can strongly influence highly heritable traits.






Important



High heritability does not mean environmental interventions are ineffective.






Consider two populations.


Everyone has:

Similar diet
Similar healthcare
Similar lifestyle

Environmental variation is small.
Therefore:
\[
V_E
\]
is relatively small.
Heritability tends to be higher.



Individuals experience:

Different diets
Unequal healthcare
Different socioeconomic conditions

Environmental variation is larger.
Therefore:
\[
V_E
\]
increases.
Heritability decreases.





This means:

The same trait can have different heritability estimates in different populations.

Heritability depends on:

Geography
Historical period
Age
Ancestry
Environmental exposure

This is why heritability estimates should always be interpreted in the context of the population being studied.




A useful conceptual diagram is:
Phenotypic Variation
        │
        ├── Genetic
        │
        └── Environmental
As we will see later, both genetic and environmental influences can themselves be partitioned into multiple components.




Estimating heritability helps answer important scientific questions.


How much of disease risk is genetic?
Examples:

Schizophrenia
Depression
Alzheimer’s disease
Type 2 diabetes




How much variation in cognitive ability is genetic?
How important is family environment?



Can interventions reduce disease risk even for highly heritable traits?



Which plant or animal traits should be selected in breeding programs?





Modern heritability theory originates from the work of Ronald A. Fisher.
In 1918, Fisher showed how Mendelian inheritance could explain continuously distributed traits such as height.
This work laid the foundation for modern quantitative genetics.




Monozygotic (MZ) twins share:
100% of their DNA
Dizygotic (DZ) twins share approximately:
50% of their segregating DNA
Yet both typically grow up in similar family environments.
This creates a powerful framework for separating genetic and environmental influences.




Throughout this tutorial we will build the following framework:
Phenotypic Variance
        ↓
A, C, and E Components
        ↓
Twin Correlations
        ↓
Falconer's Formula
        ↓
Structural Equation Models
        ↓
ACE Models
        ↓
OpenMx
        ↓
Genetic Relatedness
        ↓
GRM
        ↓
SNP Heritability





Heritability measures the proportion of variance attributable to genetic differences.
Heritability is a population-level quantity.
Heritability does not describe how genetic a trait is for an individual.
High heritability does not imply environmental interventions are ineffective.
Phenotypic variance can be partitioned into genetic and environmental components.
Twin studies provide one of the most powerful approaches for estimating heritability.
Understanding variance decomposition is the foundation for ACE models and modern genomic analyses.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
2.1 Introduction
In Part 1, we learned that phenotypic variance can be partitioned into genetic and environmental components:
\[
V_P = V_G + V_E
\]
This is an important starting point, but it is still too simplistic.
Neither genetic variance nor environmental variance is a single entity.
Instead, both can be decomposed into multiple components, each representing a different biological mechanism.
The classical twin design and Structural Equation Models (SEM) attempt to estimate these components separately.
Understanding these components is the foundation of:

Twin studies
ACE models
ADE models
OpenMx analyses
SNP heritability
Modern quantitative genetics

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
2.2 Decomposing Phenotypic Variance
A more complete model is:
\[
V_P = V_A + V_D + V_C + V_E
\]
where:



Component
Meaning




\(V_A\)
Additive genetic variance


\(V_D\)
Dominance genetic variance


\(V_C\)
Shared environmental variance


\(V_E\)
Unique environmental variance



This decomposition appears repeatedly throughout twin modeling and quantitative genetics.

text:
2.3 A Useful Analogy
Imagine baking a cake.
The final cake represents:
\[
V_P
\]
The ingredients represent:

Genetics
Family environment
Personal experiences

Different ingredients contribute differently to the final outcome.
Similarly, phenotypic variation arises from multiple sources.

3.1 What Does “Additive” Mean?
Additive genetics refers to the cumulative effect of individual alleles.
Each allele contributes a small amount to the phenotype.
These contributions simply add together.
Hence the name:

Shared environmental effects make family members more similar.
These are influences that individuals living in the same family experience together.

6.1 What Is Unique Environment?
Unique environmental effects make family members different.
Even identical twins experience unique events.
Examples:

Different friends
Different illnesses
Different teachers
Different accidents
Different life experiences

Even monozygotic twins are never perfectly identical.

Therefore:
\[

+
Measurement Error

text:
12.1 Key Takeaways

Phenotypic variance can be partitioned into multiple components.
Additive effects (A) represent cumulative allele effects.
Dominance effects (D) represent non-additive allele interactions.
Shared environment (C) makes family members more similar.
Unique environment (E) makes family members different.
Measurement error is included in E.
ACE models estimate A, C, and E.
ADE models estimate A, D, and E.
Understanding these components is essential before studying twin correlations.

text:
13.1 Introduction
In Part 2, we learned that phenotypic variance can be decomposed into:
\[

\]
or, in some situations,
\[
V_P = V_A + V_D + V_E
\]
The next question is:

How can we estimate these components from real data?

The answer lies in one of the most elegant designs in all of genetics:

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
13.2 The Classical Twin Design
Twin studies provide a natural experiment that allows us to separate genetic and environmental influences.
The key insight is simple:

Monozygotic twins share more genetic material than dizygotic twins, while both typically share similar family environments.

By comparing how similar these two types of twins are, we can infer how much variation is due to genetics and how much is due to environment.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
113.1 Introduction
In Parts 1–6, we learned how twin studies estimate:

Additive genetic effects (A)
Shared environmental effects (C)
Unique environmental effects (E)

using differences in similarity between monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twins.
However, there is an important caveat:

Twin studies do not directly observe A, C, and E.

Instead, they infer these components from observed patterns in the data.
This inference is only valid if several assumptions hold.
Every statistical model relies on assumptions.
Twin studies are no exception.
Before interpreting heritability estimates, we must understand:

What assumptions are being made?
Why are they necessary?
What happens if they are violated?

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
section: 116.1 What Is the Equal Environment Assumption?
text:
116.1 What Is the Equal Environment Assumption?
The Equal Environment Assumption states:

Environmental similarity is approximately the same for MZ and DZ twins.

This is arguably the most important assumption in twin research.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
116.2 Why Is It Needed?
Recall:
MZ twins share:
\[
100\%
\]
of their DNA.
DZ twins share:
\[
50\%
\]
of their DNA.
The twin method assumes:
The major difference between MZ and DZ twins is genetic similarity.
If MZ twins also experience substantially more similar environments, then increased similarity could be mistakenly attributed to genetics.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
116.3 Example
Suppose parents:

Dress MZ twins identically
Give them identical toys
Encourage identical activities

but do not treat DZ twins similarly.
Then:
MZ twins become more similar
for environmental reasons.
The twin model might incorrectly interpret this as genetic influence.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
116.4 Visual Illustration

116.4.1 Ideal Situation
MZ Twins
   ↑
Same Environment

DZ Twins
   ↑
Same Environment
Only genetics differs.



116.4.2 Problematic Situation
MZ Twins
   ↑↑↑
Much More Similar Environment

DZ Twins
   ↑
Less Similar Environment
Environmental effects become confounded with genetic effects.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
116.5 Does EEA Hold?
Many studies have tested the EEA.
Results generally suggest:

MZ twins are treated somewhat more similarly
However, this typically explains only a small portion of observed twin resemblance

The assumption appears reasonably robust for many traits.
Nevertheless, it should never be ignored.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
117.1 What Is Random Mating?
The twin model assumes that mate selection is random with respect to the trait.
For example:
Tall individuals
are assumed not to systematically choose:
Other tall individuals

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
117.2 Why Does This Matter?
Suppose highly educated individuals preferentially marry other highly educated individuals.
This phenomenon is called:

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text: 117.3 Assortative Mating

text:
118.1 Consequences
If assortative mating exists:
DZ twins may share more than the expected:
\[
50\%
\]
of trait-related genetic variation.
This increases:
\[
r_{DZ}
\]
and can inflate estimates of:
\[
C
\]
while reducing estimates of:
\[
A
\]

With assortative mating:

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
119.1 What Is Gene–Environment Correlation?
Genes can influence the environments individuals experience.
This creates:

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
119.2 Gene–Environment Correlation
often abbreviated:
rGE

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
119.3 Example
Suppose a child inherits musical talent.
That child may:

Practice more
Join music programs
Receive encouragement from teachers

The environment becomes correlated with genetics.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
119.4 Three Types of rGE

119.4.1 Passive rGE
Parents provide:

Genes
Environment

simultaneously.
Example:
Musical parents provide both musical genes and musical environments.



119.4.2 Evocative rGE
Individuals evoke responses from others.
Example:
A naturally sociable child receives more social interactions.



119.4.3 Active rGE
Individuals seek environments that match their genetic predispositions.
Example:
Athletic individuals seek sports activities.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
119.5 Why This Matters
The ACE model assumes:
Genes
and
Environment
are independent.
Gene–environment correlation violates this assumption.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
120.1 What Is Gene–Environment Interaction?
A gene–environment interaction occurs when:

The effect of a gene depends on the environment.

or

The effect of an environment depends on genotype.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
120.2 Example
Consider a genetic predisposition for obesity.
Under:
Healthy Diet
the genetic effect may be small.
Under:
High-Calorie Diet
the same genetic predisposition may become much stronger.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
120.3 Mathematical View
Without interaction:
\[
Phenotype
=
Gene
+
Environment
\]
With interaction:
\[
Phenotype
=
Gene
+
Environment
+
Gene \times Environment
\]

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
120.4 Why This Matters
Classical ACE models assume:
\[
G\times E=0
\]
If interactions exist:
variance components may be misestimated.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
121.1 Example
Problematic design:
MZ twins from one country

DZ twins from another country
Differences may reflect:

Culture
Environment
Sampling

rather than genetics.

text:
121.2 Desired Situation
MZ and DZ twins sampled from the same population.

text:
122.1 Example
Suppose a study includes only:
Highly educated families

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
122.2 Why This Matters
Remember:
Heritability depends on:

Population
Environment
Historical context

Biased sampling can distort estimates.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
123.1 Consequences of Misclassification
Suppose some DZ twins are incorrectly labeled as MZ.
Observed:
\[
r_{MZ}
\]
decreases.
This may reduce estimated:
\[
A
\]
and inflate:
\[
E
\]

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
123.2 Modern Approaches
Historically:

Questionnaires
Physical resemblance

were used.
Today:

SNP genotyping
DNA-based relatedness

provide highly accurate classification.

title: From Twin Correlations to Heritability: A Complete Introduction to ACE Models, SEM, and Genetic Relatedness
text:
124.1 Equal Environment Assumption
to be the most critical assumption.
Why?
Because violations directly affect the comparison between:
\[
r_{MZ}
\]
and
\[
r_{DZ}

This discrepancy became known as:

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS): From GWAS to Genetic Prediction
text:
Over the last two decades, Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) have revolutionized our understanding of the genetic architecture of complex traits and diseases. Researchers have identified thousands of genetic variants associated with conditions such as schizophrenia, coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, depression, and many other common disorders.
Unlike Mendelian diseases, which are often caused by mutations in a single gene, most common diseases are influenced by a very large number of genetic variants, each contributing only a tiny effect. This phenomenon is known as polygenicity.
The realization that thousands of variants collectively influence disease risk led to the development of one of the most important tools in modern statistical genetics:
Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS).
A Polygenic Risk Score combines information across many genetic variants into a single numerical value that represents an individual’s inherited genetic predisposition to a trait or disease.
In this tutorial we will learn:

Prediction
The ultimate goal is accurate prediction of phenotypes.

Linear Regression Revisited
Consider ordinary linear regression:
$ y = X+ e $
where:

\(y\) = phenotype
\(X\) = genotype matrix
\(\beta\) = SNP effects
\(e\) = residual error

In GWAS we often estimate one SNP at a time.
BLUP takes a different approach.
Instead of fitting millions of separate regressions:
SNP1 → Trait
SNP2 → Trait
SNP3 → Trait
BLUP fits all SNPs simultaneously.


The Mixed Model Framework
BLUP is usually formulated as a linear mixed model.
The model becomes:
\[
y = Xb + Zu + e
\]
where:

\(Xb\) represents fixed effects
\(Zu\) represents genetic effects
\(e\) represents residual error


Fixed Effects
Fixed effects include known covariates:

Sex
Age
Principal Components
Batch Effects

Example:
\(Xb=Age + Sex + PC1 + PC2\).
These effects are estimated directly.



Random Effects
The genetic component is treated as a random effect.
\(u \sim N(0,G\sigma_g^2)\)
where:

\(G\) is the Genetic Relationship Matrix (GRM)
\(\sigma_g^2\) is genetic variance

This assumption is central to BLUP.
Instead of estimating each SNP independently, BLUP models their collective contribution.


The Genetic Relationship Matrix (GRM)
One of the most important concepts in BLUP is the Genetic Relationship Matrix.
The GRM measures genetic similarity between individuals.
Suppose we have three people:



Person
Relationship




A vs A
1.0


A vs B
0.10


A vs C
0.02


B vs C
0.08



These values form a matrix:
\(G =\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0.10 & 0.02 \
0.10 & 1 & 0.08 \
0.02 & 0.08 & 1
\end{bmatrix}\)
The matrix summarizes how genetically similar individuals are.


Why Use the GRM?
The intuition is simple.
If genetics influences a trait:
More Genetically Similar
            ↓
More Phenotypically Similar
BLUP uses this relationship to estimate genetic effects.

Shrinkage
A key feature of BLUP is shrinkage.
Instead of trusting GWAS estimates completely, BLUP pulls effect sizes toward zero.
Suppose GWAS estimates:



SNP
GWAS Effect




rs1
0.40


rs2
0.05


rs3
0.01

SNP
BLUP Effect




rs1
0.25


rs2
0.03


rs3
0.005



Large effects are reduced.
Small effects are reduced even more.
This process decreases noise and improves prediction.



Why Shrinkage Helps
Imagine estimating SNP effects from a small sample.
Some estimates become large simply by chance.
Without shrinkage:
Signal + Noise
With shrinkage:
Mostly Signal
BLUP reduces overfitting by shrinking noisy estimates toward zero.


BLUP Polygenic Scores
After estimating SNP effects, PRS calculation is unchanged.
We still compute:
\(PRS_i=\sum_j\hat{\beta}*j x*{ij}\).
The difference is:
C+PT
↓

versus
BLUP
↓
All SNPs
Every SNP contributes to the final score.


Advantages of BLUP
BLUP offers several improvements over C+PT.

Uses All SNPs
No information is discarded.


No Arbitrary P-value Thresholds
No need to choose:
P < 0.01
P < 0.05
P < 0.1


Handles Polygenicity Naturally
Works well when many variants contribute small effects.


Reduced Overfitting
Shrinkage improves stability.



Limitations of BLUP
Despite its strengths, BLUP has important limitations.


Assumes All SNPs Have Effects
BLUP assumes \(\beta_j \neq 0\) for every SNP.
Reality is often different.
Many SNPs likely have no effect at all.


Assumes a Single Normal Distribution
All SNP effects come from one distribution \(N(0,\sigma_\beta^2)\).
Complex traits may contain:

Null SNPs
Small-effect SNPs
Medium-effect SNPs
Large-effect SNPs

A single distribution may be unrealistic.

Limited Flexibility
BLUP cannot easily model:

Sparse architectures
Functional annotations
Different effect-size classes

These limitations motivated Bayesian methods.
