BLUP was a major advance because it demonstrated that using all SNPs can improve prediction.


From BLUP to Bayesian Methods
Researchers soon realized that the assumptions of BLUP were often too restrictive.
Questions emerged:

What if many SNPs have zero effect?
What if effect sizes come from multiple distributions?
What if we want to include biological annotations?

Answering these questions led to Bayesian approaches such as:

BayesA
BayesB
BayesC
BayesR
SBayesR
SBayesRC

These methods generalize the BLUP framework while relaxing its assumptions.


Key Takeaways

BLUP is a whole-genome regression method.
BLUP assumes all SNPs contribute small effects.
SNP effects are assumed to follow a normal distribution.
BLUP uses all SNPs simultaneously.
The method relies on a Genetic Relationship Matrix (GRM).
Shrinkage reduces overfitting and improves prediction.
BLUP eliminates the need for clumping and p-value thresholding.
The infinitesimal model is both BLUP’s strength and its limitation.
Modern Bayesian methods evolved directly from the BLUP framework.



Bayesian Methods for Polygenic Prediction
In the previous chapter, we explored Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (BLUP), one of the first whole-genome regression approaches for polygenic prediction.
BLUP represented a major advance over Clumping and P-value Thresholding (C+PT) because it:

Uses all SNPs simultaneously
Models genome-wide effects
Applies shrinkage to reduce noise
Eliminates arbitrary p-value thresholds

However, BLUP makes a strong assumption:

Every SNP has a non-zero effect drawn from the same normal distribution.

Reality is often more complicated.
Some SNPs may have:

No effect
Tiny effects
Moderate effects
Large effects

This observation motivated the development of Bayesian methods, which provide a more flexible framework for modeling genetic architecture.
Modern approaches such as:

BayesA
BayesB
BayesC
BayesR
SBayesR
SBayesRC

all originate from Bayesian statistics.
Understanding the Bayesian framework is therefore essential for understanding modern polygenic prediction.

Why Bayesian Methods?
Suppose we analyze one million SNPs.
BLUP assumes \(\beta_j \sim N(0,\sigma_\beta^2)\).
for every SNP.
This means:
text id="k7ybj4" SNP1 → Small Effect SNP2 → Small Effect SNP3 → Small Effect ... SNP1,000,000 → Small Effect
While reasonable for highly polygenic traits, this assumption is often unrealistic.
In reality:
Many SNPs → No Effect

Some SNPs → Tiny Effect

Few SNPs → Moderate Effect

Very Few SNPs → Large Effect
Bayesian models can represent this complexity.



The Bayesian Philosophy
Classical statistics treats parameters as fixed but unknown quantities.
For example:
\[
\beta = 0.05
\]
We do not know its value, but we assume a single true value exists.
Bayesian statistics takes a different view.
It treats parameters as random variables.
Instead of asking:

What is the value of β?

we ask:

What is the probability distribution of β?

This seemingly small change has enormous consequences.

Prior Beliefs
Bayesian analysis begins with a prior distribution.
A prior represents our beliefs before seeing the data.
For example:
Suppose we believe most SNPs have effects close to zero.
We might write:
\[
\beta_j \sim N(0,\sigma^2)
\]
This prior expresses our belief that:

Most effects are small
Positive and negative effects are equally likely
Large effects are rare



Data Provides Evidence
Next we observe data.
For example:



SNP
GWAS Effect




rs1
0.05


rs2
0.01


rs3
0.00



The data contribute information through the likelihood function.
The likelihood answers:

How probable is the observed data if a particular parameter value were true?




Bayes’ Theorem
Bayesian inference combines:

Prior beliefs
Observed data

using Bayes’ theorem.
In words:
text id="8bx8i2" Posterior = Prior Information + Observed Data
The posterior distribution represents our updated beliefs after observing the data.

Understanding the Posterior Distribution
Suppose our prior believes:
β ≈ 0
but the GWAS strongly suggests:
β ≈ 0.3
The posterior combines both sources of information.
Result:
β ≈ 0.2
The final estimate lies somewhere between prior expectations and observed evidence.


Why This Is Useful
GWAS estimates are noisy.
Especially when sample sizes are limited.
Suppose a SNP has:
\[
\hat{\beta}=0.4
\]
This estimate may be inflated by chance.
Bayesian methods naturally shrink estimates toward plausible values.
Instead of:
0.40
the posterior estimate may become:
text id="7l8v6v" 0.22
This often improves prediction accuracy.


From BLUP to Bayesian Models
BLUP uses a single normal prior:
\[
\beta_j \sim N(0,\sigma_\beta^2)
\]
Bayesian methods allow more flexible priors.
For example:
Many SNPs:
β = 0

Some SNPs:
Small Effects

Few SNPs:
Large Effects
These assumptions often better match biological reality.


Sparse Genetic Architecture
Consider a trait influenced by:

100 causal variants
1,000,000 measured SNPs

Most SNPs have \(\beta = 0\).
BLUP struggles because it assumes every SNP contributes.
Bayesian models can explicitly represent sparsity.
This is one reason they often outperform BLUP.


BayesC: The First Important Bayesian Model
One of the most influential models is BayesC.
BayesC assumes:
Some SNPs have no effect:
\[
\beta_j = 0
\]
while others have non-zero effects:
\(\beta_j \sim N(0,\sigma_\beta^2)\).
The model becomes:
\[
\beta_j=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{with probability }\pi \
N(0,\sigma_\beta^2) & \text{with probability }1-\pi
\end{cases}
\]
This is known as a spike-and-slab prior.

Understanding the Spike-and-Slab Prior
Imagine a distribution consisting of two parts.
Spike
|
|
|
|
0
Most SNPs belong here.
They have exactly zero effect.
The second part:
Slab
contains SNPs with non-zero effects.
This simple idea dramatically improves flexibility.




Why BayesC Improves Prediction?
BayesC recognizes that:
text id="jsyepm" Many SNPs ↓ No Effect
Rather than forcing every SNP to contribute.
This leads to:

Less noise
Better shrinkage
Improved prediction

especially when the true genetic architecture is sparse.

The Challenge of Posterior Inference
Unfortunately, Bayesian models are mathematically complex.
The posterior distribution usually cannot be solved directly.
There is no closed-form solution.
Instead we must approximate the posterior.
This leads to one of the most important tools in Bayesian statistics:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).


Why MCMC Is Needed?
Consider millions of SNPs.
Each SNP has:

An unknown effect
An unknown inclusion status

The number of possible parameter combinations becomes enormous.
Direct calculation becomes impossible.
Instead we generate samples from the posterior distribution.


Intuition Behind MCMC
Imagine exploring a landscape.
text id="9jjlwm" High Posterior Probability          ^          |        Peak       /   \      /     \
The algorithm spends more time near regions of high posterior probability.
Over many iterations, sampled values reconstruct the posterior distribution.


The Basic BayesC Algorithm
Initialize:
text id="hr8t53" β σ²β σ²e π
Then repeatedly:

Update SNP effects
Update genetic variance
Update residual variance
Update inclusion probability

Repeat thousands of times.
Eventually the chain converges.



Trace Plots
One way to assess convergence is through trace plots.
A trace plot shows sampled values across iterations.
Good convergence looks like:
text id="9zck4h" Stable fluctuations around a constant mean
Poor convergence looks like:
text id="2xibqe" Upward trend or downward trend
indicating the chain has not stabilized.

Posterior Means
After convergence:
We summarize the posterior using:
\[
E(\beta_j|Data)
\]
This posterior mean becomes the final SNP effect estimate.
These estimates are then used to calculate Polygenic Risk Scores.



Why Bayesian Methods Often Outperform BLUP?
Bayesian models can:

Represent sparse architectures
Model multiple effect-size classes
Perform adaptive shrinkage
Better reflect biological reality

As a result they often produce:
text id="7sv2lm" Higher Prediction Accuracy
than BLUP.

The Evolution of Bayesian Models
BayesC was only the beginning.
Researchers later developed:
BayesA
All SNPs have effects.
Heavy-tailed prior.
BayesB
Many SNPs have zero effects.
Non-zero SNPs follow a separate distribution.
BayesC
Spike-and-slab prior.
Computationally simpler.
BayesR
Multiple effect-size distributions.
More realistic architecture.
SBayesR
Summary-statistics implementation of BayesR.
SBayesRC
Extends SBayesR by incorporating functional annotations.



Summary
Bayesian methods transformed polygenic prediction by allowing more realistic assumptions about genetic architecture.
Instead of assuming:
text id="v1ib1m" All SNPs have small effects
Bayesian approaches allow:
```text id=“l3fd3d” Many SNPs → Zero Effect
Some SNPs → Small Effect
Few SNPs → Large Effect

This flexibility often leads to improved prediction accuracy.

Modern methods such as SBayesR and SBayesRC represent the current state of the art in polygenic prediction and are direct descendants of these Bayesian ideas.

#### Key Takeaways

* Bayesian methods treat SNP effects as random variables.
* Prior distributions encode biological assumptions.
* Bayes' theorem combines prior information and observed data.
* The posterior distribution represents updated beliefs.
* BayesC introduces the spike-and-slab prior.
* Bayesian methods naturally model sparse genetic architectures.
* MCMC sampling is used when posterior distributions cannot be solved analytically.
* Posterior means provide SNP effect estimates.
* Bayesian methods generally outperform BLUP when genetic architectures are complex.
* Modern methods such as SBayesR and SBayesRC are built on Bayesian foundations.


### Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC): The Engine Behind Bayesian Polygenic Prediction

In the previous chapter, we introduced Bayesian methods for polygenic prediction and learned how models such as BayesC use prior distributions and Bayes' theorem to estimate SNP effects.

A major challenge immediately appeared:

> The posterior distribution cannot usually be calculated directly.

For simple statistical models, posterior distributions may have closed-form solutions.

Unfortunately, polygenic prediction is not a simple problem.

Modern datasets may contain:

* Millions of SNPs
* Thousands of individuals
* Multiple unknown parameters
* Complex dependency structures

The posterior distribution becomes extraordinarily complicated.

This is where one of the most powerful tools in modern statistics enters the picture:

**Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)**.

MCMC is the computational engine that makes Bayesian polygenic prediction possible.

Without MCMC, methods such as:

* BayesA
* BayesB
* BayesC
* BayesR

would be nearly impossible to implement.

#### Why Do We Need MCMC?

Suppose we want to estimate SNP effects:

$$
\beta_1,\beta_2,\ldots,\beta_m
$$

For one million SNPs:

$$
m = 1,000,000
$$

The posterior distribution becomes:

$$
P(\beta_1,\beta_2,\ldots,\beta_m|Data)
$$

This is a probability distribution in an extremely high-dimensional space.

Direct calculation is impossible.

Instead of computing the posterior exactly, we approximate it by generating samples from it.

This is the central idea behind MCMC.

##### What Is a Markov Chain?

The first part of MCMC is the **Markov Chain**.

A Markov chain is a sequence of states where:

> The next state depends only on the current state.

Not on the entire history.

For example:

```text id="yg1k1k"
State 1 → State 2 → State 3 → State 4
To determine State 4:
text id="m9t6n6" Need State 3 only
Earlier states do not matter directly.
This property is known as:

The Markov Property


Everyday Example
Imagine walking through a city.
At each intersection:

Turn left
Turn right
Go straight

Your next move depends only on your current location.
Not on the entire route you previously traveled.
This is a Markov process.

What Is Monte Carlo?
The second part of MCMC is:
Monte Carlo
Monte Carlo methods use randomness to approximate difficult calculations.
Suppose we want to estimate:
\[
\pi
\]
One approach:

Randomly throw points into a square.
Count how many land inside a circle.

As the number of points increases:
text id="9crzz7" Random Sampling         ↓ Approximation         ↓ True Value
Monte Carlo methods use the same philosophy.
Random sampling approximates difficult mathematical quantities.



Combining the Two Ideas
MCMC combines:
text id="4n4vtp" Markov Chain       + Monte Carlo
to generate samples from complicated probability distributions.
Rather than computing:
\[
P(\beta|Data)
\]
directly,
we generate many samples:
\[
\beta^{(1)}
\]
\[
\beta^{(2)}
\]
\[
\beta^{(3)}
\]
\[
\cdots
\]
These samples gradually reconstruct the posterior distribution.


Visualizing the Posterior
Imagine a posterior distribution:
text id="lz2srl"              *            *****          *********        ************* ------|------0------|------
The goal is to understand:

Shape
Mean
Variance

Instead of calculating everything analytically, MCMC generates random samples.
Over time:
text id="tjlwmh" Samples    ↓ Histogram    ↓ Posterior Distribution


The Core Idea
Suppose the posterior has regions of:

High probability
Low probability

MCMC spends:
text id="mvwskg" More Time ↓ High Probability Regions
and
text id="bz7l8v" Less Time ↓ Low Probability Regions
As a result, the sample distribution gradually resembles the true posterior.


The Bayesian Parameters in Polygenic Prediction
In BayesC, several unknown quantities must be estimated.
These include:


SNP Effects
\[
\beta
\]


Genetic Variance
\[
\sigma_\beta^2
\]


Residual Variance
\[
\sigma_e^2
\]


Inclusion Probability
\[
\pi
\]
Each parameter depends on the others.
This dependency makes direct estimation difficult.



Why Parameters Depend on Each Other
Consider one SNP.
Its estimated effect depends on:

Residual variance
Genetic variance
Inclusion probability

But:
Residual variance depends on SNP effects.
Genetic variance depends on SNP effects.
Inclusion probability depends on SNP effects.
Thus:
```text id=“29vkyy” β depends on σ²
σ² depends on β

Everything is interconnected.

#### Gibbs Sampling

The most common MCMC algorithm in Bayesian genetics is:

**Gibbs Sampling**

The idea is surprisingly simple.

Instead of estimating all parameters simultaneously:

```text id="l4n6pw"
β
σ²β
σ²e
π
we update them one at a time.

Gibbs Sampling Workflow
Start with initial values.
Example:
```text id=“1kzr0q” β = 0
σ²β = 1
σ²e = 1
π = 0.95

Then repeatedly update:

```text id="z3m6s3"
Update β
↓
Update σ²β
↓
Update σ²e
↓
Update π
↓
Repeat
Thousands of times.


One Iteration of Gibbs Sampling
Suppose we are at iteration:
text id="ivq8nq" Iteration 500
Step 1:
Update SNP effects.
text id="snn9kq" β → new value
Step 2:
Update genetic variance.
text id="ohvkqn" σ²β → new value
Step 3:
Update residual variance.
text id="qovldm" σ²e → new value
Step 4:
Update inclusion probability.
text id="9ewv1e" π → new value
Move to iteration 501.
Repeat.


Burn-In Period
Early MCMC samples are often unreliable.
The chain has not yet reached the posterior distribution.
Example:
text id="m2s0sj" Iteration 1 Iteration 2 Iteration 3
These values may depend heavily on starting conditions.
Therefore we discard them.
This discarded portion is called:

Burn-in



Example Burn-In
Suppose:
text id="tt8olz" Total Iterations = 50,000
Burn-in:
text id="mycezu" First 10,000 iterations
Retained:
text id="0f9mxy" Remaining 40,000 iterations
Only retained samples are used for inference.


Trace Plots
One of the most important diagnostic tools is the trace plot.
A trace plot shows:
text id="h5w7pc" Parameter Value        vs Iteration Number

Good Trace Plot
A well-behaved chain looks like:
text id="4ehjlwm" ~~~~~~~~~~~ ~~~~~~~~~~~ ~~~~~~~~~~~
The chain fluctuates around a stable mean.
This suggests convergence.



Bad Trace Plot
A problematic chain may look like:
text id="upfwkq" /  /   /    /
or
text id="cy1q7i" \/\/\/\/\/\/
with large trends.
Such patterns indicate poor convergence.


What Is Convergence?
Convergence means:

The chain has reached the target posterior distribution.

After convergence:
text id="vzv6hp" Samples ≈ Posterior Distribution
Inference becomes reliable.

Posterior Mean
After collecting samples:
\[
\beta^{(1)},
\beta^{(2)},
\ldots,
\beta^{(N)}
\]
we calculate:
\(\bar{\beta} =\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\beta^{(i)}\)
This posterior mean becomes the SNP effect estimate.




Posterior Variance
We can also estimate uncertainty \(Var(\beta)\).
Large variance:
text id="sgnyjd" High Uncertainty
Small variance:
text id="7uq2kw" High Confidence
This is one of the major advantages of Bayesian inference.


Posterior Inclusion Probability (PIP)
In BayesC-type models, a SNP may be:
text id="8ghn3u" Included
or
text id="awunvb" Excluded
during each iteration.
Suppose:
text id="qvgsfz" 50,000 iterations
A SNP is included:
text id="7z7ifc" 45,000 times
Then:
\(PIP=\frac{45000}{50000}= 0.90\)
This value is called the:
Posterior Inclusion Probability (PIP)


Interpreting PIP



PIP
Interpretation




0.01
Almost certainly irrelevant


0.10
Weak evidence


0.50
Moderate evidence


0.90
Strong evidence


0.99
Very strong evidence



High-PIP SNPs are strong candidate causal variants.

Computational Cost
MCMC is powerful but expensive.
Example:
text id="8zl2vq" 1 Million SNPs 50,000 Iterations
can require:

Hours
Days
Large memory resources

This computational burden motivated later developments such as:

SBayesR
SBayesRC

which operate using summary statistics and efficient matrix methods.
Strengths of MCMC
MCMC provides:

Flexible Bayesian inference
Full posterior distributions
Uncertainty estimation
Posterior inclusion probabilities
Realistic genetic architecture modeling

These strengths explain why Bayesian methods often outperform simpler approaches.
Weaknesses of MCMC
MCMC can be:

Computationally expensive
Slow to converge
Difficult to diagnose
Sensitive to poor mixing

These challenges motivated newer algorithms.
Nevertheless, MCMC remains one of the foundational tools of Bayesian genetics.


Summary
MCMC is the computational engine that makes Bayesian polygenic prediction possible.
Rather than solving complex posterior distributions analytically, MCMC approximates them through random sampling.
Methods such as BayesC repeatedly sample:

SNP effects
Genetic variance
Residual variance
Inclusion probabilities

Over many iterations, these samples reconstruct the posterior distribution.
Posterior means become SNP effect estimates, while posterior inclusion probabilities help identify important variants.
Understanding MCMC is essential for interpreting the output of modern Bayesian polygenic prediction methods.


Key Takeaways

MCMC stands for Markov Chain Monte Carlo.
MCMC approximates complex posterior distributions through sampling.
A Markov chain depends only on the current state.
Monte Carlo methods use random sampling for approximation.
Gibbs sampling is the most common MCMC algorithm in Bayesian genetics.
Burn-in samples are discarded.
Trace plots help assess convergence.
Posterior means provide SNP effect estimates.
Posterior Inclusion Probabilities (PIP) quantify SNP importance.
MCMC forms the computational foundation of BayesC, BayesR, and related methods.




SBayesR: A Modern Bayesian Method for Polygenic Prediction
In the previous chapter, we learned how summary statistics and LD reference panels made it possible to perform polygenic prediction without access to individual-level genotype data.
This development led to one of the most influential methods in modern statistical genetics:

SBayesR (Summary Statistics BayesR)

SBayesR combines:

Bayesian modeling
Summary statistics
LD information
Mixture priors

to estimate SNP effects across the entire genome.
Today, SBayesR is one of the most widely used methods for constructing Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) from GWAS summary statistics.
It serves as the foundation for even more advanced methods such as SBayesRC.


Why Was SBayesR Developed?
Earlier methods suffered from important limitations.

Clumping and P-value Thresholding (C+PT)
Problems:

Discards SNPs
Ignores joint LD structure
Requires threshold tuning

BLUP
Problems:

Assumes every SNP has an effect
Uses a single normal distribution
Cannot model sparse architectures

BayesC
Advantages:

Models sparsity
Flexible priors

Problems:

Requires individual-level data
Computationally expensive

Researchers wanted:
text id="qkzwm4" Bayesian Flexibility + Summary Statistics + Scalability
SBayesR was the answer.



The Main Idea Behind SBayesR
SBayesR starts from two inputs:

Input 1: GWAS Summary Statistics
For each SNP:

text id="r6zn6l" GWAS Summary Statistics             +         LD Matrix             ↓          SBayesR             ↓      Posterior SNP Effects             ↓             PRS


The BayesR Philosophy
Recall BLUP:
\[
\beta_j
\sim
N(0,\sigma^2)
\]
Every SNP effect comes from the same distribution.
BayesR introduced a more realistic assumption.
Instead of one distribution:
text id="5pjcbb" Small Effects Only
BayesR assumes multiple effect-size classes.


The Five-Component Mixture Prior
SBayesR uses a mixture distribution.
Mathematically:
$ j {k=1}^{K} _k N(0,_k^2) $
where:

\(\pi_k\) = probability of component k
\(\gamma_k\) = variance scaling factor

In practice, SBayesR typically uses five components.


The Five SNP Classes

Class 4 → Moderate Effect
Class 5 → Large Effect

This architecture closely resembles real GWAS observations.

#### Why Multiple Classes Matter

Imagine a trait influenced by:

* Thousands of tiny-effect variants
* Hundreds of small-effect variants
* Dozens of moderate-effect variants
* A few large-effect variants

BLUP struggles because all SNPs share one distribution.

SBayesR can assign each SNP to the most appropriate class.

This flexibility improves prediction accuracy.

#### The Role of Mixing Proportions

The parameters:

$$
\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4,\pi_5
$$

represent the proportion of SNPs in each class.

Example:

| Component       | Proportion |
| --------------- | ---------- |
| Zero Effect     | 95%        |
| Tiny Effect     | 3%         |
| Small Effect    | 1.5%       |
| Moderate Effect | 0.4%       |
| Large Effect    | 0.1%       |

This means:

Most SNPs contribute little or nothing.

A small number carry most of the signal.

#### Learning the Genetic Architecture

One of the strengths of SBayesR is that it learns these proportions directly from the data.

Instead of specifying:

```text id="k6efjr"
95% Zero Effects
the algorithm estimates:
\[
\pi
\]
during MCMC sampling.
This provides insight into the genetic architecture of the trait.


Recovering Joint SNP Effects
GWAS summary statistics contain marginal effects.
Recall:
$ b=R + $
where:

\(b\) = observed GWAS effects
\(R\) = LD matrix
\(\beta\) = joint SNP effects

SBayesR attempts to estimate \(\beta\).
using both:

GWAS effects
LD structure

This converts marginal effects into joint effects.


Why LD Must Be Modeled
Suppose:
text id="ct8rsv" rs1 ↔︎ rs2 ↔︎ rs3
are strongly correlated.
A naïve analysis may assign signal to all three SNPs.
SBayesR evaluates them jointly.
Result:
text id="22juzv" One SNP may receive most of the signal
while the others are shrunk toward zero.
This improves interpretability and prediction.


The Computational Challenge
A major obstacle is the LD matrix.
For:
text id="8gmj55" 1 Million SNPs
the full LD matrix contains \(10^{12}\).
entries.
This is enormous.


Sparse LD Matrices
Most SNPs are only correlated with nearby variants.
Therefore:
text id="wjlwmu" Most LD Values ≈ 0
SBayesR stores only important LD values.
This creates a sparse matrix representation.
Benefits:

Reduced memory
Faster computation
Improved scalability



Eigen Decomposition
Another important optimization is matrix decomposition.
The LD matrix can be written as: \(R=U \Lambda U^T\).
where:

\(U\) = eigenvectors
\(\Lambda\) = eigenvalues

This representation reduces computational burden during MCMC sampling.
Large biobank analyses would be nearly impossible without these optimizations.


MCMC in SBayesR
SBayesR still relies on Bayesian sampling.
The algorithm repeatedly updates:
text id="ty9px8" SNP Effects ↓ Mixture Membership ↓ Genetic Variance ↓ Residual Variance
This iterative process gradually reconstructs the posterior distribution.

Posterior SNP Effects
After convergence, each SNP receives:
\[
E(\beta_j|Data)
\]
the posterior mean effect.

\(PRS_i=\sum_j
\hat{\beta}*j
x*{ij}\)
This formula is identical to previous methods.
The difference lies in how the SNP effects were estimated.

Evaluating Polygenic Risk Scores
An important question is:

How do we determine whether a PRS is actually useful?

A score that predicts disease poorly has little practical value, regardless of how sophisticated the methodology used to construct it may be. Now, we will explore the most commonly used evaluation metrics in polygenic prediction and learn how researchers assess the performance of PRS models.

Why PRS Evaluation Matters
Suppose we build a PRS for schizophrenia.
After calculating scores for thousands of individuals, we obtain values such as:



Individual
PRS




Person A
0.52


Person B
-0.13


Person C
1.21



These numbers by themselves are meaningless.
The important question is:

Do individuals with higher PRS actually have a higher probability of developing schizophrenia?

Evaluating prediction performance allows us to determine:

Whether the PRS contains useful information
How much variation in the phenotype can be explained
Whether the PRS improves prediction beyond traditional risk factors
Whether a more sophisticated method actually performs better



Evaluating Quantitative Traits
For quantitative traits such as:

Height
BMI
Blood pressure
Cholesterol levels

the most common evaluation metric is \(R^2\), which measures the proportion of phenotypic variance explained by the model.
The ISG workshop identifies prediction \(R^2\) as the primary metric for quantitative traits.

Understanding Variance Explained
Consider human height.Suppose height varies substantially within a population. A useful PRS should explain some of this variation.
For example:
Observed Height Variation
│
├── Genetics
├── Environment
└── Random Effects
If the PRS captures part of the genetic component, it should reduce unexplained variation.
The proportion of variance explained is quantified by \(R^2\).



The Null Model
Before including PRS, researchers usually fit a model containing only covariates.Typical covariates include:

Sex
Age
Population principal components (PCs)
Recruitment center
Batch effects

The null model is: \(y = Covariates + e\),
where:

\(y\) is the phenotype
\(e\) is residual error



The Full Model
Next, we include the PRS.
The full model becomes \(y = Covariates + PRS + e\).
If PRS contains predictive information, the model should explain more variance.


Incremental R²
A crucial concept in polygenic prediction is Incremental R².
Rather than reporting the total model R², researchers usually calculate:
$$ Incremental R^2 ================

SBayesRC: Incorporating Biological Knowledge into Polygenic Prediction
In the previous chapter, we explored SBayesR, one of the most successful Bayesian methods for constructing Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) from GWAS summary statistics.
SBayesR improved prediction by:

Using all SNPs simultaneously
Modeling linkage disequilibrium (LD)
Applying Bayesian shrinkage
Using mixture distributions for SNP effects

However, SBayesR makes an important assumption:

Every SNP is treated equally before observing the data.

From a biological perspective, this assumption is unlikely to be true.
Consider two SNPs:



SNP
Location




rs1
Protein-coding exon


rs2
Intergenic region



Would we expect both SNPs to have the same probability of being causal?
Probably not.
Decades of molecular biology have shown that some genomic regions are much more likely to influence phenotype than others.
This observation motivated the development of:
SBayesRC (Summary Statistics BayesR with Functional Annotations)


Why Biological Information Matters
The human genome contains roughly:
\[
3.2 \times 10^9
\]
base pairs.
Only a small fraction directly encodes proteins.
Many genomic regions differ dramatically in biological importance.
Examples include:

Protein-coding exons
Promoters
Enhancers
Transcription factor binding sites
Conserved regions
Regulatory elements

A SNP located in one of these regions may be more likely to influence phenotype than a randomly selected variant.


The Central Question
Suppose we observe two SNPs with similar GWAS evidence.



SNP
P-value




rs1
1e-5


rs2
1e-5



If rs1 lies inside a highly conserved coding region while rs2 lies in a biologically inactive region:
Should both SNPs receive the same prior probability of being causal?
SBayesRC says:

No.



What Are Functional Annotations?
Functional annotations describe biological properties of genomic regions.
Examples include:



Annotation
Meaning




Coding
Protein sequence


Promoter
Gene regulation


Enhancer
Expression regulation


Conserved
Evolutionarily important


DHS
Open chromatin


Histone Marks
Regulatory activity



Each SNP may belong to one or more annotation categories.


Example Annotation Matrix
Suppose we have:



SNP
Coding
Promoter
Conserved




rs1
1
0
1


rs2
0
1
0


rs3
0
0
0



This annotation matrix becomes an additional source of information for the model.


The Key Idea Behind SBayesRC
Recall SBayesR:
$ _j _k _k N(0,_k^2) $
The prior probabilities are identical for every SNP.
SBayesRC modifies this assumption.
Instead, \(\pi_k=f(Annotations)\).
The probability that a SNP belongs to a particular effect-size class now depends on its biological annotation.

Intuition
Suppose:
Coding SNP
and
Intergenic SNP
have identical GWAS evidence.
SBayesRC may assign:
Coding SNP
↓
Higher Prior Probability
of having a non-zero effect.
This allows biological knowledge to influence statistical inference.


Why This Can Improve Prediction
GWAS data are noisy.
Many SNPs show weak signals.
Biological annotations provide an additional source of evidence.
Instead of relying solely on:
GWAS Signal
SBayesRC uses:
GWAS Signal
+
Biological Knowledge
This often improves estimation of SNP effects.


Heritability Enrichment
A central concept in SBayesRC is:
Heritability Enrichment
The idea is simple.
Some annotation categories explain disproportionately large amounts of heritability.
For example:



Annotation
SNP Fraction
Heritability Fraction




Coding
2%
10%


Conserved
5%
20%


Intergenic
50%
20%



Coding regions contribute more heritability than expected by chance.


Measuring Enrichment
Enrichment is calculated as:
\(Enrichment = \frac{
\text{Heritability Proportion}
}{
\text{SNP Proportion}
}\)
Example: \(\frac{0.10}{0.02}=5\).
An enrichment value of 5 indicates that the annotation contributes five times more heritability than expected.



Why Enrichment Matters
Annotations with high enrichment are more likely to contain causal variants.
SBayesRC uses this information to prioritize SNPs during Bayesian inference.
Consequently:
Highly Enriched Regions
↓
Higher Prior Probability
of contributing to disease risk.

The SBayesRC Workflow
The workflow is:
GWAS Summary Statistics
          +
LD Matrix
          +
Functional Annotations
          ↓
        SBayesRC
          ↓
 Posterior SNP Effects
          ↓
          PRS
Compared with SBayesR, the only additional input is:
Functional Annotations

Types of Annotations Used
Large studies often use:

BaselineLD annotations
Coding regions
Conserved regions
Regulatory annotations
Histone modifications
Gene-expression annotations

Modern implementations may include dozens or even hundreds of annotation categories.



Why SBayesRC Often Outperforms SBayesR?
SBayesR learns from:
Statistical Evidence
SBayesRC learns from:
Statistical Evidence
+
Biological Evidence
This additional information frequently improves prediction accuracy.
The improvement is often modest but consistent across many traits.


Real-World Interpretation
Imagine two SNPs with identical GWAS significance.
Traditional models see:
Equal Evidence
SBayesRC sees:
Equal Statistical Evidence
+
Different Biological Plausibility
The model can therefore make more informed decisions.


Limitations
Despite its advantages, SBayesRC is not perfect.


Annotation Quality Matters
Poor annotations can reduce performance.


Computational Complexity
More parameters must be estimated.


Population Differences
Annotations may not behave identically across ancestries.


Incomplete Biology
Current annotations capture only a fraction of biological complexity.


SBayesRC vs SBayesR



Feature
SBayesR
SBayesRC




Summary Statistics
Yes
Yes


LD Modeling
Yes
Yes


Mixture Priors
Yes
Yes


Functional Annotations
No
Yes


Heritability Enrichment
No
Yes


Biological Prioritization
No
Yes






Key Takeaways

SBayesRC extends SBayesR by incorporating functional annotations.
Not all SNPs are biologically equivalent.
Annotation information modifies prior probabilities of SNP effects.
Heritability enrichment identifies biologically important genomic regions.
SBayesRC combines statistical and biological evidence.
Functional annotations often improve prediction accuracy.
SBayesRC represents one of the most advanced PRS methods currently available.



Practical Polygenic Risk Score Analysis: PRSice, GCTB, SBayesR and SBayesRC
In the previous chapters, we developed the theoretical foundations of polygenic prediction.
We have learned:

What Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) are
How PRS are evaluated
Clumping and P-value Thresholding (C+PT)
BLUP
Bayesian methods
MCMC
SBayesR
SBayesRC

Now it is time to connect theory with practice.
In this chapter we will walk through a complete PRS workflow using tools commonly employed in modern statistical genetics:

PLINK
PRSice
GCTB
SBayesR
SBayesRC

By the end of this chapter you should understand how GWAS summary statistics are transformed into Polygenic Risk Scores that can be applied to new individuals.

The Complete PRS Pipeline
Most modern PRS analyses follow the workflow below:
text id="n4q9ii" Discovery GWAS         ↓ Summary Statistics QC         ↓ PRS Method (C+PT / SBayesR / SBayesRC)         ↓ Posterior SNP Effects         ↓ PLINK Scoring         ↓ Polygenic Scores         ↓ Prediction Evaluation
Every PRS method ultimately produces:
text id="1xg2qe" SNP Effects
which are then combined with target genotypes.

A complete PRS analysis usually requires three datasets.


Discovery Dataset
Used to perform GWAS.
Produces:

to model linkage disequilibrium.

Step 4: Creating an LD Reference for SBayesR

\(PRS_i=\sum_j

for every individual.

Now evaluate PRS performance.

Phenotype ~ Sex + Age + PCs + PRS
Compare against:
Phenotype ~ Sex + Age + PCs

measures genetic predictive value.

Example in Python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

null_model.fit(X_cov, y)
r2_null = r2_score(y, null_model.predict(X_cov))

full_model.fit(X_full, y)
r2_full = r2_score(y, full_model.predict(X_full))

incremental_r2 = r2_full - r2_null

print(incremental_r2)

Method

Common Problems

Allele Mismatches

Best Practices
Always:

These practices ensure reliable prediction estimates.


Key Takeaways

PRS analysis consists of GWAS, effect estimation, scoring, and evaluation.
PRSice implements Clumping and P-value Thresholding.
GCTB implements SBayesR and SBayesRC.
SBayesR requires summary statistics and LD references.
SBayesRC additionally requires functional annotations.
PLINK converts SNP effects into individual Polygenic Risk Scores.
Incremental R² is commonly used to assess prediction accuracy.
Independent validation is essential for avoiding inflated results.




Interpreting Polygenic Risk Scores: What Do They Really Mean?
After spending several chapters learning how Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) are constructed, optimized, and evaluated, we now arrive at perhaps the most important question:

What does a Polygenic Risk Score actually mean?

This question is surprisingly difficult.
Many people assume that a high PRS means:
You will get the disease.
or that a low PRS means:
You are protected.
Neither statement is correct.
A Polygenic Risk Score is fundamentally a statistical predictor, not a diagnosis.
Understanding what PRS can and cannot tell us is essential for responsible use in research, medicine, and public health.


What a PRS Measures
Recall the standard formula:
\(PRS_i=\sum_j
\hat{\beta}*j x*{ij}\)
A PRS combines information across many genetic variants into a single number.
The resulting score represents:

An individual’s relative genetic predisposition compared with others in the same population.

Notice the word:
relative
A PRS does not directly measure disease.
Instead, it measures inherited genetic burden.


An Analogy: Height Prediction
Imagine we create a PRS for height.
Suppose:



Person
PRS




A
-2.1


B
0.0


C
+2.4



Would we know their exact heights?
No.
However, we might predict:
Person C
↓
Likely Taller
than
Person A
The PRS provides information about relative position within the population.
The same logic applies to disease risk.


Relative Risk Versus Absolute Risk
One of the most important distinctions in genetic prediction is:

Relative Risk
versus


Absolute Risk
These terms are often confused.



Relative Risk
Suppose the average disease risk is:
\[
10%
\]
A PRS study reports:
text id="iwjlwm" Top PRS Decile ↓ 3× Higher Risk
This means:
\(10% \times 3=30%\)
The individual’s relative risk increased threefold.


Absolute Risk
The actual probability becomes:
\[
30%
\]
Notice:
30%
≠
100%
Even high-risk individuals may never develop the disease.
This distinction is crucial when communicating PRS results.

PRS Percentiles
Raw PRS values are difficult to interpret.
Example:



Individual
PRS




A
-0.78


B
0.13


C
1.42



What does:
PRS = 1.42
actually mean?
By itself:
Almost Nothing
Interpretation becomes easier using percentiles.


Understanding Percentiles
Suppose a population contains:
100,000 individuals
A PRS percentile represents position within the distribution.
Examples:



Percentile
Meaning




1st
Lower than 99% of people


50th
Population average


90th
Higher than 90% of people


99th
Higher than 99% of people



Percentiles are often far more intuitive than raw scores.


Visualizing a PRS Distribution
Most PRS follow an approximately normal distribution.
                *
              *****
            *********
          *************
--------|-----50%-----|--------
Most individuals cluster near the middle.
Extreme scores occur less frequently.


Risk Stratification
A common strategy is to divide individuals into groups.
Example:



Group
PRS Range




Bottom 10%
Lowest scores


Middle 80%
Average scores


Top 10%
Highest scores



Researchers then compare disease prevalence.


Example: Coronary Artery Disease
Suppose:



Group
Disease Rate




Bottom 10%
3%


Average
7%


Top 10%
18%



Interpretation:
text id="0m4wjv" Higher PRS ↓ Higher Disease Frequency
However:
Most High-PRS Individuals
Still Do Not Develop Disease


Odds Ratios
Risk differences are often summarized using odds ratios.
Suppose:



Group
Odds Ratio




Bottom Decile
1.0


Top Decile
3.5



Interpretation:
Individuals in the highest PRS group have:
$ 3.5 $
times greater disease odds than individuals in the lowest group.
Notice:
Odds
≠
Probability
These concepts are related but not identical.


PRS Is Not Destiny
One of the biggest misconceptions about genetic prediction is:

Genes determine everything.

This is false.
Most phenotypes arise from:
$Phenotype=
Genetics + Environment + Random Effects $
Even highly heritable diseases are influenced by non-genetic factors.



Example: Type 2 Diabetes
Genetic risk matters.
However:

Diet
Physical activity
Obesity
Smoking
Sleep

also contribute substantially.
A person with:
High PRS
may never develop disease.
Conversely:
Low PRS
does not guarantee protection.


Heritability Places an Upper Limit
Recall from earlier chapters:
Prediction accuracy is constrained by heritability.
Suppose:
\[
h^2 = 0.40
\]
Only 40% of phenotypic variation is genetic.
Even a perfect PRS cannot explain:
\[
100%
\]
of disease risk.
This limitation is fundamental.


What Does a High PRS Actually Mean?
A high PRS generally suggests:

Increased inherited susceptibility
Elevated relative risk
Greater likelihood of disease compared with the population average

It does not imply:

Certainty of disease
Immediate clinical diagnosis
Presence of symptoms

These distinctions are essential.


Clinical Interpretation
Researchers are increasingly interested in clinical applications.
Potential uses include:

Early Screening
Identify individuals at elevated risk before symptoms appear.


Preventive Medicine
Target interventions toward high-risk individuals.


Risk Communication
Combine genetic and environmental information.



Personalized Medicine
Adjust treatment strategies according to risk profiles.
However, clinical implementation remains an active area of research.


Population Differences
One of the most important limitations of PRS is portability.
Suppose a PRS is trained using:
European GWAS
and applied to:
African Population
Prediction accuracy often decreases substantially.


Why Does This Happen?
Several factors contribute:

Different allele frequencies
Different LD patterns
Different environmental exposures
Different genetic architectures

As a result:
Same PRS
↓
Different Performance
Across Populations
This remains one of the major challenges in human genetics.


PRS and Individual Decision Making
Should individuals make major life decisions based solely on PRS?
Generally:
No
PRS should be viewed as one piece of information among many.
Clinical decisions should also consider:

Family history
Lifestyle
Environmental exposures
Medical records
Biomarkers

PRS is most powerful when integrated with other risk factors.


Ethical Considerations
As genetic prediction becomes more common, important ethical questions arise.

Privacy
Who owns genetic information?


Discrimination
Could PRS influence insurance or employment decisions?


Communication
How should risk information be explained responsibly?


Equity
How can benefits be shared across diverse populations?
These questions remain active areas of discussion.



Common Misinterpretations

Misinterpretation 1
text id="2oqnmu" High PRS = Disease
Incorrect.


Misinterpretation 2
Low PRS
=
Protected
Incorrect.


Misinterpretation 3
Genetics
=
Destiny
Incorrect.


Misinterpretation 4
PRS Works Equally
In Every Population
Incorrect.



Integrating Genetics and Environment
The future of prediction likely involves combining:
Genetics
+
Lifestyle
+
Environment
+
Clinical Variables
rather than relying on genetics alone.
Such integrated models often outperform PRS-only approaches.


Key Takeaways

A PRS measures relative genetic predisposition.
PRS is not a diagnosis.
Relative risk and absolute risk are different concepts.
Percentiles often provide the most intuitive interpretation.
High PRS does not guarantee disease.
Low PRS does not guarantee protection.
Environmental factors remain critically important.
Prediction accuracy is limited by heritability.
PRS performance often varies across populations.
Clinical use requires careful interpretation and communication.


Summary
Polygenic Risk Scores are powerful tools for summarizing inherited genetic risk.
However, interpretation requires caution.
A PRS is best viewed as a probabilistic indicator of susceptibility rather than a deterministic prediction of future outcomes.
Understanding this distinction is essential for researchers, clinicians, and individuals who may eventually use PRS in real-world settings.



The Future of Polygenic Risk Scores: Multi-Ancestry Prediction, Functional Genomics, and Precision Medicine
Over the course of this tutorial series, we have journeyed from the basic concept of Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) to some of the most advanced prediction methods currently available, including SBayesR and SBayesRC.
We have learned:

How GWAS identifies genetic associations
How Polygenic Risk Scores are constructed
Why linkage disequilibrium matters
How Bayesian methods improve prediction
The role of functional annotations
How PRS should be interpreted

The natural question now becomes:

Where is the field heading next?

Despite remarkable progress, today’s PRS methods are still far from perfect.
Several major challenges remain:

Limited portability across ancestries
Missing heritability
Gene-environment interactions
Rare variants
Clinical implementation

These challenges are driving the next generation of statistical genetics research.

The Current State of Polygenic Prediction
Today’s best-performing PRS methods can achieve impressive prediction accuracy for many traits.
Examples include:



Trait
Typical Predictive Performance




Height
High


BMI
Moderate


Coronary Artery Disease
Moderate


Type 2 Diabetes
Moderate


Schizophrenia
Moderate


Depression
Lower



However, prediction accuracy varies substantially across traits and populations.
The reasons behind these differences provide important clues about future developments.


The Multi-Ancestry Problem
One of the largest challenges in modern statistical genetics is ancestry portability.
Most large GWAS have been conducted in individuals of European ancestry.
Consequently:
text id="e7hr0f" European GWAS         ↓ European PRS
often performs well.
However:
text id="wjlwm8" European GWAS         ↓ African Population
usually results in reduced prediction accuracy.


Why Does Portability Decline?
Several biological factors contribute.


Allele Frequencies Differ
A SNP common in Europeans may be rare in Africans.
Example:



SNP
European Frequency
African Frequency




rs1
40%
5%



Prediction performance can therefore change dramatically.


Different LD Patterns
Linkage Disequilibrium structures vary between populations.
For example:
text id="35j0t7" European LD rs1 ↔︎ rs2
may become:
text id="jlwm24" African LD rs1   rs2
with much weaker correlation.
Methods relying on LD therefore lose predictive power.


Environmental Differences
Environmental exposures differ across populations.
Examples include:

Diet
Healthcare access
Education
Socioeconomic conditions

Consequently:
text id="bd2v2j" Same Genetics + Different Environment = Different Outcomes


Multi-Ancestry PRS
Researchers are increasingly developing:
Multi-Ancestry PRS
These methods combine data from multiple ancestral groups.
Goal:
text id="qux0lw" More Diverse GWAS         ↓ Better Generalization
Modern approaches attempt to model:

Shared genetic effects
Population-specific effects
Shared biological pathways

simultaneously.


Larger GWAS Sample Sizes
Prediction accuracy is strongly influenced by discovery sample size.
As GWAS datasets continue to grow:
text id="3rl5zs" More Samples         ↓ More Accurate Effect Estimates         ↓ Better PRS
Biobanks now contain:



Resource
Approximate Size




UK Biobank
~500,000


All of Us
~1,000,000 planned


FinnGen
~500,000


Million Veteran Program
>1,000,000



Future datasets may include tens of millions of individuals.


Rare Variants
Most current PRS focus on common variants.
However:
text id="jlwm4t" Rare Variants
may have larger biological effects.
Traditional GWAS often struggles to identify them because:

They are uncommon
Statistical power is limited

Future PRS models will likely integrate:

Common variants
Rare variants
Structural variants

into a unified framework.


Functional Genomics
Current PRS methods increasingly use biological annotations.
However, today’s annotations remain incomplete.
Future prediction models may incorporate:


Gene Expression
eQTL information.


Chromatin Accessibility
Open chromatin regions.


Single-Cell Data
Cell-type specific effects.


Epigenetics
DNA methylation and histone modifications.
The future model may look like:
text id="jlwm61" GWAS + Expression + Epigenetics + Single Cell Data         ↓ Enhanced PRS


Transcriptome-Wide Prediction
One exciting direction involves integrating genetically predicted gene expression.
Examples include:

TWAS
PrediXcan
FUSION

Instead of predicting disease directly from SNPs:
text id="jlwm72" SNPs ↓ Gene Expression ↓ Disease
These methods may provide more biologically interpretable predictions.


Gene-Environment Interactions
Traditional PRS models assume:
text id="jlwm83" Genetics + Environment
contribute independently.
Reality is often more complex.
Example:
A genetic predisposition for obesity may be amplified by:

High-calorie diets
Sedentary lifestyle

but reduced by:

Exercise
Healthy nutrition

This phenomenon is known as:
Gene-Environment Interaction (G×E)


Future Prediction Models
Future risk prediction may incorporate:
text id="jlwm94" Genetics + Environment + Lifestyle + Biomarkers + Medical History
rather than relying on genetics alone.
Such integrated models may substantially outperform PRS-only approaches.



Machine Learning and Deep Learning
Another rapidly growing area involves artificial intelligence.
Researchers are investigating:

Neural networks
Graph neural networks
Transformer architectures
Deep representation learning

for genomic prediction.
Potential advantages:

Capture nonlinear effects
Model complex interactions
Integrate multiple data types

However:
Current evidence suggests that for many PRS applications:
text id="jlwma5" Better Data > More Complex Models
Thus, data quality often matters more than model complexity.


Clinical Implementation
Perhaps the most exciting frontier is clinical translation.
Potential applications include:

Cardiovascular Disease
Earlier intervention for high-risk individuals.


Cancer Screening
Risk-based screening programs.


Psychiatry
Early identification of vulnerable individuals.


Preventive Medicine
Personalized prevention strategies.



Challenges to Clinical Adoption
Several obstacles remain.

Calibration
Predicted risks must correspond to actual outcomes.


Equity
Prediction should work across diverse populations.


Interpretation
Clinicians require understandable outputs.


Ethics
Privacy and fairness concerns must be addressed.
These challenges are as important as statistical performance.



Precision Medicine
The long-term vision is:
text id="jlwmb6" Individual Genome         + Environment         + Medical History         ↓ Personalized Healthcare
This concept is often referred to as:
Precision Medicine
PRS may become one component of future personalized healthcare systems.

The Missing Heritability Problem
Even the best PRS does not explain all genetic influences.
Many factors remain difficult to capture:

Rare variants
Structural variation
Gene interactions
Epigenetics
Environmental modulation

Understanding these factors remains an active research area.


What Will PRS Look Like in 10 Years?
A future PRS may combine:
text id="jlwmc7" Common Variants + Rare Variants + Functional Genomics + Gene Expression + Epigenetics + Environment
into a single integrated prediction model.
Prediction accuracy is likely to improve substantially as larger datasets and richer biological information become available.


Lessons From This Tutorial Series
Polygenic prediction has evolved through several generations of methods:



Era
Method




Early
Candidate Genes


GWAS Era
Single SNP Analysis


PRS Era
C+PT


Whole Genome Era
BLUP


Bayesian Era
BayesR


Summary Statistics Era
SBayesR


Functional Genomics Era
SBayesRC



Each generation incorporated more information and more realistic assumptions.



Final Key Takeaways

PRS has become one of the central tools of modern statistical genetics.
Prediction accuracy continues to improve as datasets grow.
Multi-ancestry prediction remains a major challenge.
Functional genomics is becoming increasingly important.
Rare variants represent an important future direction.
Gene-environment interactions remain largely unexplained.
Deep learning may contribute but is not a complete solution.
Clinical implementation requires careful validation.
Precision medicine is a long-term goal rather than a current reality.
Future prediction models will likely integrate genetics, biology, environment, and clinical data.

Polygenic Risk Scores represent one of the most successful applications of statistical genetics in the genomic era.
What began as simple weighted sums of GWAS effects has evolved into sophisticated Bayesian models capable of integrating linkage disequilibrium, functional annotations, and massive biobank datasets.
Although significant challenges remain, the field continues to advance rapidly. The combination of larger datasets, richer biological annotations, multi-ancestry studies, and improved statistical methods is steadily moving us closer to more accurate and clinically useful genetic prediction.
For researchers entering statistical genetics today, understanding PRS provides a foundation for exploring many of the most exciting developments in genomics, precision medicine, and computational biology.

title: Multivariate Concepts in Statistical Genetics: From LD Score Regression to Genomic SEM
text:
Multivariate Concepts in Statistical Genetics
In many areas of statistical genetics, we are not only interested in whether a single trait is heritable. We are also interested in whether multiple traits share part of their genetic architecture.
For example, psychiatric traits such as major depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia are not genetically isolated. They often show genetic overlap. This means that some genetic variants may influence more than one phenotype.
This tutorial introduces the main multivariate concepts needed to understand Genomic SEM. We will move step by step from basic ideas such as polygenicity and LD Score Regression to genetic covariance, genetic correlation, genome-wide structural models, and multivariate GWAS.

1. Why Do We Need Multivariate Genetic Models?
Complex traits are usually highly polygenic. This means that they are influenced by thousands of genetic variants, each with a very small effect.
A simple single-gene model is usually not appropriate for complex psychiatric or behavioral traits. Instead, risk emerges from the combined effect of many variants.
This creates two important problems:

We need methods that can summarize genome-wide genetic signal.
We need methods that can estimate how much genetic signal is shared across traits.

This is where LD Score Regression and Genomic SEM become useful.


2. From Genetic Overlap to Genetic Architecture
Genetic overlap means that the same genetic variants contribute to variation in more than one phenotype.
However, genetic overlap can appear in different forms.
Two traits may share:
A broad common genetic factor Several smaller domain-specific factors A mixture of shared and trait-specific genetic effects SNPs that influence one trait much more than another
Genomic SEM allows us to model these possibilities explicitly.
For example, if four psychiatric traits are genetically correlated, we can test whether this correlation is well explained by one common factor.
A simplified model could be:
$ F_1 MDD, PTSD, ANX, ALCH $
where \((F_1)\) is a shared genetic liability factor.


3. Why Traits Do Not Need to Come From the Same Sample
One powerful feature of LD Score Regression and Genomic SEM is that traits do not need to be measured in the same individuals.
For example, we may have:
A GWAS of major depression from one cohort A GWAS of anxiety from another cohort A GWAS of PTSD from another cohort A GWAS of alcohol use disorder from another cohort
These GWAS may come from different studies, different consortia, and different individuals.
The connection between them is the genome.
Because each GWAS reports SNP-level effects across the genome, we can compare the pattern of SNP effects across traits. If SNPs that increase one trait also tend to increase another trait, this creates evidence of shared genetic architecture.
This is why summary statistics are so useful. We do not always need access to individual-level data to study genetic overlap.


2. Polygenicity and Linkage Disequilibrium
Suppose a phenotype is influenced by a few true causal variants. In GWAS, we do not observe only those causal variants. We also observe many nearby SNPs that are correlated with them.
This correlation among SNPs is called linkage disequilibrium, or LD.
A SNP with high LD is correlated with many nearby SNPs. Therefore, high-LD SNPs are more likely to tag causal variants. This means they are more likely to show association signal even if they are not causal themselves.

2.1 LD Score
The LD score of SNP (j) is defined as:
$ _j = i r{ij}^2 $
where:

\(\ell_j\) is the LD score of SNP (j)
\(r_{ij}^2\) is the squared correlation between SNP (i) and SNP (j)

A high LD score means that the SNP is correlated with many other SNPs.



4. The Intuition Behind LD Score Regression
LD Score Regression works because highly polygenic traits create a predictable relationship between LD and GWAS signal.
Imagine there are true causal variants in the genome.
A SNP does not need to be causal to show association. If it is correlated with a causal variant through LD, it can still pick up association signal.
This means:
High-LD SNPs are correlated with many nearby SNPs. Therefore, they have more chances to tag causal variants. Low-LD SNPs are correlated with fewer nearby SNPs. Therefore, they usually only show strong signal if they are causal or very close to causal variants.
For a highly polygenic trait, many causal variants are spread across the genome. As a result, SNPs with higher LD scores tend to have larger GWAS chi-square statistics on average.
This is the core logic of LD Score Regression.


5. Why the LDSC Intercept Matters
In GWAS, test statistics can be inflated for several reasons.
Some inflation reflects true polygenic signal. This is expected when many SNPs contribute to the trait.
However, some inflation can come from confounding, such as:
Population stratification Cryptic relatedness Sample overlap Technical artifacts
LD Score Regression separates these components.
The slope of the regression captures polygenic signal.
The intercept captures inflation that is not explained by LD score.
This is why LD Score Regression is useful: it helps distinguish true polygenic signal from confounding.


3. SNP Heritability Using LD Score Regression
LD Score Regression is based on a simple idea:
If a trait is highly polygenic, SNPs with higher LD scores should, on average, have larger GWAS test statistics.
In other words, we regress the GWAS chi-square statistics on LD scores.
The expected chi-square statistic for SNP (j) can be written as:
$ E[_j^2 | _j] = _j + Na + 1 $
where:

\(N\) is the GWAS sample size
\(h^2\) is SNP heritability
\(M\) is the number of SNPs
\(\ell_j\) is the LD score
\(a\) captures confounding such as population stratification
the intercept captures inflation not due to polygenic signal

The slope of this regression is used to estimate SNP heritability.

3.1 Why Sample Size Matters
Imagine two traits have the same GWAS p-values, but different sample sizes:

Trait 1: \(N = 50,000\)
Trait 2: \(N = 100,000\)

If the association statistics are similar, the trait with the smaller sample size may imply stronger per-sample genetic signal. This is why LD Score Regression accounts for sample size when estimating heritability.



4. Genetic Covariance and Genetic Correlation
LD Score Regression can also be extended to two traits.
Instead of regressing one trait’s chi-square statistics on LD scores, we examine the product of GWAS (Z)-statistics across two traits.
For traits (Y_1) and (Y_2), we use:
$ Z_{1j}Z_{2j} $
If SNPs with high LD scores tend to have similar effects across both traits, this suggests genetic overlap.

4.1 Genetic Covariance
Genetic covariance measures the extent to which two traits share genetic influences.
The cross-trait LD Score Regression equation is:
$ E[z_{1j}z_{2j}|_j] = j + + {Ns} $
Conceptually:

The slope estimates genetic covariance.
The intercept captures sample overlap and confounding.
Traits do not need to be measured in the same individuals.

This is very useful because many GWAS summary statistics are publicly available and come from independent cohorts.


4.2 Genetic Correlation
Genetic correlation is the standardized form of genetic covariance:
$ r_g = {} $
A genetic correlation close to 1 means two traits share much of their genetic architecture.
A genetic correlation close to 0 means little shared genetic influence.
A negative genetic correlation means genetic variants that increase one trait tend to decrease the other.

### 8. Why Shared Genetic Architecture Requires New Models





5. From LD Score Regression to Genomic SEM
Genomic SEM stands for Genomic Structural Equation Modeling.
It provides a flexible framework for fitting structural equation models to genetic covariance matrices estimated from GWAS summary statistics.
The main advantage is that we can model genetic relationships among traits even when those traits were measured in different samples.


6. The Two-Stage Framework of Genomic SEM
Genomic SEM has two main stages.

Stage 1: Estimate Genetic Covariance Structure
Using multivariable LD Score Regression, we estimate:

A genetic covariance matrix
A sampling covariance matrix

The genetic covariance matrix is usually called (S).
The diagonal elements of (S) are SNP heritabilities.
The off-diagonal elements are genetic covariances.
A simplified matrix looks like this:
$ S =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
h^2_1 & cov_{g,12} & cov_{g,13} \\
cov_{g,12} & h^2_2 & cov_{g,23} \\
cov_{g,13} & cov_{g,23} & h^2_3
\end{bmatrix}\]
$


Stage 2: Fit a Structural Equation Model
After estimating (S), we fit a model to explain the covariance structure.
For example, we may fit a common factor model where depression, anxiety, PTSD, and alcohol use disorder load on a shared internalizing factor.



9. Genome-Wide SEM vs Multivariate GWAS
It is important to distinguish between genome-wide SEM and multivariate GWAS.

Genome-Wide SEM
Genome-wide SEM uses the genetic covariance matrix across traits.
It asks:
What is the genetic relationship among these traits?
For example:
Do the traits load on one common factor? Are there multiple factors? Does one genetic trait predict another? How well does the model fit?
This stage does not test SNP effects directly.


Multivariate GWAS
Multivariate GWAS adds SNP effects to the model.
It asks:
Which SNPs are associated with the latent genetic factor?
For example:
$ F_1 SNP $
This tests whether each SNP predicts the shared genetic factor.
So, genome-wide SEM models the covariance structure, while multivariate GWAS tests SNP-level effects on that structure.



7. Practical Setup in R
We will now follow the practical structure from the workshop.
The main steps are:

Load GenomicSEM
Munge GWAS summary statistics
Run LD Score Regression
Specify and run a genome-wide Genomic SEM model
Prepare summary statistics for multivariate GWAS
Run userGWAS
Interpret factor GWAS and QSNP results

)

The matrix LDSC_INT$S contains genetic variances and covariances.

10. Factor Identification in Genomic SEM
Latent factors do not have a natural scale. Therefore, we must identify the scale of the factor.
There are two common approaches.
Option 1: Unit Variance Identification
In this approach, the variance of the latent factor is fixed to 1.
Example:
Model <- ” F1 =~ NAMDD + PTSD + ALCH + ANX F1 ~~ 1F1 ”
This means the factor has a standardized variance.
In Genomic SEM, this is often equivalent to using:
std.lv = TRUE Option 2: Unit Loading Identification
In this approach, one factor loading is fixed to 1.
Example:
Model <- ” F1 =~ 1*MDD + PTSD + ALCH + ANX ”
Here, the scale of the factor is defined by MDD.
Both approaches are valid, but they lead to different parameter scaling. The interpretation of the model should always consider how the factor was identified.


13. Lavaan Model Syntax Used in Genomic SEM
Genomic SEM uses lavaan-style model syntax.
Here are the most important operators:



Syntax
Meaning




A ~ B
A is regressed on B


A ~~ A
Variance of A


A ~~ B
Covariance between A and B


F1 =~ A + B + C
Latent factor F1 loads on A, B, and C


A ~~ 1*B
Fix covariance between A and B to 1


A ~~ a*B
Label covariance as parameter a



This syntax allows us to specify many different genetic models.


14. Common Factor Model
A common factor model assumes that several observed traits share one underlying latent genetic factor.
For example:
$ F1 MDD, PTSD, ALCH, ANX $
Here, F1 represents a shared internalizing genetic factor.

# Define covariance structure
covstruc <- LDSC_INT

# Common factor model
INT.model <- "
F1 =~ MDD + PTSD + ALCH + ANX
"

# Use unit variance identification
std.lv <- TRUE

# Run model
IntResults <- usermodel(
  covstruc = covstruc,
  model = INT.model,
  std.lv = std.lv
)

15. Genetic Multiple Regression
Genomic SEM is not limited to factor models. It can also estimate genetic regression models.
For example, suppose we want to know whether the genetic component of educational attainment is associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
A simplified model could be:
[ EA_g = b_1SCZ_g + b_2BIP_g + u]
This means that the genetic component of educational attainment is regressed on the genetic components of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
In lavaan-style syntax, this could be written as:
model <- ” EA ~ SCZ + BIP SCZ ~~ BIP ”
This allows us to ask whether one trait explains unique genetic variation in another trait after accounting for additional genetically correlated traits.


16. GWAS-by-Subtraction
GWAS-by-subtraction is one of the important applications of Genomic SEM.
The idea is to separate shared and residual genetic components.
For example, educational attainment and cognitive performance are genetically correlated. But educational attainment is influenced by both cognitive and non-cognitive factors.
A Genomic SEM model can estimate:
A cognitive genetic factor shared with cognitive performance A non-cognitive genetic component of educational attainment
Conceptually:
$ EA = Cognitive + NonCognitive $
This allows researchers to perform GWAS on the residual non-cognitive component.
In simple terms, GWAS-by-subtraction asks:
What genetic signal remains in one trait after removing the genetic signal shared with another trait?
This is useful when we want to isolate more specific genetic pathways.

Model fit tells us whether the proposed model explains the observed genetic covariance matrix well.
Important fit statistics include:

Chi-square: lower is better
AIC: useful for comparing models
CFI: higher is better
SRMR: lower is better

As a rough guide:

CFI > 0.90 suggests acceptable fit
CFI > 0.95 suggests good fit
SRMR < 0.10 suggests acceptable fit
SRMR < 0.05 suggests good fit

17. Interpreting the Common Factor Model
A strong loading of MDD on F1 means that major depression strongly reflects the shared genetic factor.
A weaker loading of ALCH on F1 means that alcohol use disorder may share some genetic risk with the factor, but also has more trait-specific genetic influences.
The residual variance of each trait represents genetic variation not explained by the common factor.

20. Multivariate GWAS in Genomic SEM
So far, we estimated a genome-wide model using the genetic covariance matrix.
Now we move to multivariate GWAS.
The goal is to test SNP effects on a latent factor.
Instead of asking:

Is this SNP associated with MDD?

we ask:

Is this SNP associated with the shared genetic factor underlying MDD, PTSD, ALCH, and ANX?

This can increase power and improve interpretation when traits share genetic architecture.


21. Steps for Multivariate GWAS
Multivariate GWAS in Genomic SEM has four main steps:

Munge summary statistics
Run LD Score Regression
Prepare summary statistics using sumstats
Run multivariate GWAS using userGWAS

The first two steps are the same as before. If we already ran LDSC for the same traits, we do not need to repeat it.


22. Step 3 for Multivariate GWAS: Prepare SNP Summary Statistics
The sumstats() function prepares SNP-level summary statistics for userGWAS.
In the workshop practical, reduced chromosome 4 files are used for demonstration.

# Prepare summary statistics

23. Why linprob Is Needed
Sometimes binary traits are analyzed as continuous outcomes, or the summary statistics contain only Z-statistics.
In these cases, Genomic SEM needs additional information to reconstruct the appropriate beta and standard error.
In this practical, linprob = TRUE is used for ALCH.


24. Step 4: Run userGWAS
Now we run a multivariate GWAS.
The model is:
$ F1 =~ MDD + PTSD + ALCH + ANX $
and then:
$ F1 SNP $
This tests whether each SNP predicts the shared latent genetic factor.

# Covariance structure from LDSC
covstruc <- LDSC_INT

# SNP-level summary statistics
SNPs <- INT_sumstats

# Multivariate GWAS model
model <- "
F1 =~ MDD + PTSD + ALCH + ANX
F1 ~ SNP
"

# Save only the SNP effect on F1
sub <- "F1~SNP"

# Practical uses serial processing
parallel <- FALSE

# Calculate QSNP
Q_SNP <- TRUE

# Run multivariate GWAS
INT_GWAS <- userGWAS(
  covstruc = covstruc,
  SNPs = SNPs,
  model = model,
  sub = sub,
  parallel = parallel,
  Q_SNP = Q_SNP
)

28. QSNP: Testing SNP-Level Heterogeneity
QSNP tests whether the SNP effect fits the common pathway model.
If a SNP acts mainly through the common factor, then its effects on individual traits should be consistent with the factor structure.
If the SNP has a strong trait-specific effect, the common pathway model may not fit well.
A significant QSNP value suggests SNP-level heterogeneity.
This means the SNP may affect one or more traits differently than expected from the common factor model.
QSNP can be used in two ways:
As a quality-control metric As a biological result
As a QC metric, it can help identify SNPs that do not cleanly represent the common factor.
As a biological result, it can highlight SNPs that differentiate related traits.


29. QSNP as a QC Metric
Suppose a SNP is significantly associated with an internalizing factor.
If QSNP is not significant, this suggests that the SNP effect is consistent with the shared factor.
But if QSNP is highly significant, the SNP may not be a clean factor SNP.
It may be driven mainly by one phenotype.
For example, a SNP may look associated with an internalizing factor, but the effect may actually be much stronger for depression than anxiety or PTSD.
In that case, QSNP warns us that the SNP may have trait-specific effects.


30. QSNP as a Biological Result
QSNP is not only a warning. It can also be scientifically interesting.
A significant QSNP result may reveal SNPs that distinguish traits that are otherwise genetically correlated.
For example, depression and anxiety may share a broad genetic factor, but some variants may be more specific to depression.
Similarly, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder may share genetic liability, but some variants may help differentiate them.
Therefore, QSNP can be used to study genetic specificity within broader shared genetic architecture.


31. Multiple-Factor Models and QSNP
In models with multiple factors, QSNP can be calculated for each SNP-factor relationship.
This is useful because a SNP may fit one factor well but show heterogeneity for another factor.
For example, a SNP may operate cleanly through a substance-use factor but show disorder-specific effects within an internalizing factor.
This makes QSNP especially useful in complex psychiatric models where several correlated factors are estimated together.

29. Interpreting QSNP
QSNP can be interpreted in two ways.
First, it can be used as a quality-control metric. If a SNP has a strong factor association but also a very significant QSNP value, the SNP may not represent the common factor cleanly.
Second, QSNP can be a result of interest. It may identify SNPs that differentiate traits from one another.
For example, a SNP may be associated with depression but not anxiety, even though both traits load on the same internalizing factor.

35. Important Practical Advice
Genomic SEM is flexible, but this flexibility should be used carefully.
Do not simply try many models until one gives a significant result.
A better workflow is:

Define your research question.
Write down your hypothesized model.
Run the model.
Check model fit.
Interpret parameters cautiously.
If using data-driven exploration, clearly report it as exploratory.

This is especially important in multivariate genetic modeling because many reasonable models may appear plausible.


36. Summary
In this tutorial, we covered the main concepts behind multivariate genetic analysis using Genomic SEM.
We learned that complex traits are highly polygenic and that LD Score Regression uses the relationship between LD score and GWAS signal to estimate SNP heritability.
We then extended this idea to genetic covariance and genetic correlation across traits.
Finally, we introduced Genomic SEM as a framework for fitting structural models to genetic covariance matrices and for running multivariate GWAS on latent genetic factors.
The key idea is simple but powerful:

Instead of studying each trait separately, Genomic SEM allows us to model shared and trait-specific genetic architecture across multiple traits.

This makes it especially useful for psychiatric, behavioral, anthropometric, and medical traits where genetic overlap is common.


37. Key Takeaways

Complex traits are usually highly polygenic.
LD scores summarize how much LD each SNP has with nearby SNPs.
LD Score Regression estimates SNP heritability from GWAS summary statistics.
Cross-trait LD Score Regression estimates genetic covariance and genetic correlation.
Genomic SEM fits structural equation models to genetic covariance matrices.
A common factor model can capture shared genetic liability across traits.
Multivariate GWAS can test SNP effects on latent genetic factors.
QSNP tests whether SNP effects are consistent with the common factor model or show trait-specific heterogeneity.

title: Mendelian Randomization
text:
One of the fundamental goals of science is to determine whether one variable causes another. In medicine, epidemiology, genetics, economics, and social sciences, researchers often observe relationships between variables. However, observing a relationship is not the same as proving a causal effect.
For example:
These observations are informative, but they do not automatically establish causality.
Understanding the distinction between correlation and causation is one of the most important concepts in statistics and epidemiology. It is also the motivation behind Mendelian Randomization, a powerful approach that uses genetic variants to investigate causal relationships.

title: Causation in Statistical Genetics
text:
Limited Statistical Power
A single SNP usually explains only a tiny proportion of variation in the exposure.
For example:

One BMI-associated SNP may explain less than 0.1% of BMI variation.

This limits precision.

title: Causation in Statistical Genetics
text:
Sensitivity to Random Error
Any measurement error in the SNP-exposure or SNP-outcome estimate directly affects the causal estimate.

title: Causation in Statistical Genetics
text:
Vulnerability to Pleiotropy
If the SNP violates one of the MR assumptions, the entire analysis becomes biased.
For these reasons, modern MR studies typically use many genetic instruments.

title: Mendelian Randomization
text:
Single SNP
With one SNP:
[ IVW = Wald Ratio]

title: Mendelian Randomization
text:
Multiple SNPs
With multiple SNPs:
[ IVW ===
Weighted Average of Wald Ratios ]
Thus, IVW can be viewed as a natural extension of the Wald Ratio.

Why IVW Became the Standard Method
IVW became the most widely used MR estimator because it offers several advantages.

Higher Statistical Power
Using many SNPs substantially increases power.


Greater Precision
Combining information reduces uncertainty.


Easy Interpretation
The estimate has a straightforward causal interpretation.


Computational Simplicity
IVW is easy to implement and computationally efficient.



The Assumptions Behind IVW
IVW relies on the same three instrumental variable assumptions introduced in Part 2.

Assumption 1: Relevance
Each SNP must be associated with the exposure.
[ SNP Exposure]


Assumption 2: Independence
Each SNP must be independent of confounders.
$ SNP Confounders $


Assumption 3: Exclusion Restriction
Each SNP must affect the outcome only through the exposure.
$ SNP Exposure Outcome $
and not through alternative pathways.



The Problem of Horizontal Pleiotropy
IVW performs very well when all instruments are valid.
However, if some SNPs affect the outcome through pathways other than the exposure, bias may occur.
For example:
$ SNP Exposure Outcome $
but also:
$ SNP Outcome $
This phenomenon is called horizontal pleiotropy.
Horizontal pleiotropy is one of the major threats to Mendelian Randomization.
Later tutorials will introduce methods specifically designed to address this problem.

Fixed Effects and Random Effects IVW
In practice, two versions of IVW are commonly used.

Fixed Effects IVW
Assumes all SNPs estimate exactly the same causal effect.
Differences among SNP estimates are attributed solely to sampling variation.



Random Effects IVW
Allows some additional heterogeneity among SNP estimates.
Random effects models are often preferred when mild pleiotropy or heterogeneity is suspected.



Example from Modern Genetic Epidemiology
Suppose researchers want to determine whether BMI causally influences coronary heart disease.
A GWAS identifies hundreds of SNPs associated with BMI.
For each SNP:

Obtain SNP → BMI effects.
Obtain SNP → CHD effects.
Calculate Wald ratios.
Combine them using IVW.

The resulting IVW estimate provides an overall causal estimate of BMI on coronary heart disease risk.
This workflow forms the foundation of many modern Mendelian Randomization studies.

Strengths of IVW

High statistical power.
Increased precision.
Uses all available instruments.
Straightforward interpretation.
Widely accepted in genetic epidemiology.



Limitations of IVW

Sensitive to pleiotropy.
Requires valid instruments.
Can be biased when assumptions are violated.
Does not automatically detect directional pleiotropy.

Because of these limitations, IVW is usually accompanied by additional sensitivity analyses.



Looking Ahead
The IVW method is often the starting point of a Mendelian Randomization analysis.
However, researchers must also investigate whether the IVW assumptions are reasonable.
One major concern is horizontal pleiotropy.
In the next tutorial, we will introduce:

Horizontal pleiotropy
Why it threatens causal inference
Visualizing pleiotropic pathways
Detecting violations of MR assumptions

This will prepare us for robust methods such as MR-Egger, Weighted Median, and Weighted Mode estimators.


Key Takeaways

Modern Mendelian Randomization studies usually use multiple SNPs.
Each SNP produces a Wald Ratio estimate.
IVW combines these estimates using inverse variance weighting.
More precise instruments receive larger weights.
IVW can be interpreted as a weighted average of Wald Ratios.
IVW is the standard MR estimator used in many studies.
Horizontal pleiotropy remains an important challenge.
Sensitivity analyses are required to assess robustness.
